species.name: Aplysina cauliformis
species.description:
Lilac creeping morphotype
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A slender, branching sponge with a rope-like form that grows in long, thin, sinuous strands. The branches spread irregularly in many directions and often intertwine, loop, or sprawl horizontally across the surface. Colonies can look like a loose tangle of cords spread over rocks or coral.
Growth form:
Branches are long, cylindrical, and narrow — usually about the thickness of a finger or pencil.
They extend in irregular directions and often bend or curve sharply rather than growing straight.
Growth often spreads outward across the substrate rather than vertically.
Branches may cross over each other or form messy, net-like clusters.
Color:
Always purple to lavender in color, sometimes slightly bluish.
Color is uniform along the branches, though tips can appear a little paler or more translucent.
Consistent across colonies — not mottled or patchy.
Surface features:
Smooth to slightly uneven surface, sometimes with faint swellings or constrictions along the branch.
Many small, round pores visible on the surface, often arranged in neat rows running along the length of the branches.
Each pore usually has a thin, raised rim, visible even in close-up photos.
Visual context clues:
Frequently seen lying across rocks, coral heads, or rubble like ropes draped on the surface.
The branching pattern appears messy and asymmetrical, with arms spreading outward or sideways.
Colonies can form dense tangles that sprawl over more than a meter of substrate.

species.name: Aplysina fulva
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A tall, elegantly branching sponge with slender, elongated branches that are characteristically golden-yellow to mustard-yellow in colour, often with darker tan or olive tones at the base and along lower portions of branches. The colony grows upright and somewhat spreading, with a loose, delicate branching architecture that resembles a miniature tree or tree-like structure. Individual branches are relatively thin and wiry, typically 0.5 to 1.5 cm in diameter, and taper gradually toward the tips, which are blunt or slightly rounded. The overall impression is of a gracefully vertical structure occupying a distinct three-dimensional space on the reef, with considerable open space between branches.
Growth form:
•          Develops from a relatively narrow base (2 to 5 cm wide) that firmly attaches to rock or coral with a single or dual main axis.
•          Primary branches extend upward and outward in a roughly conical or fan-like silhouette, each dividing dichotomously (splitting into two subequal branches) 1 to 3 times.
•          Secondary and tertiary branches remain relatively parallel to the primary axis direction, creating an ordered, tree-like branching pattern rather than a chaotic tangle.
•          Branch spacing increases with height: lower branches are closely packed, while upper branches spread more widely, with inter-branch gaps of 1 to 5 cm.
•          The entire colony typically reaches 30 to 60 cm in height and 20 to 40 cm in width at the widest spreading point.
•          Branch tips are blunt to slightly rounded, never sharp or pointed, and do not subdivide further into fine branchlets.
•          Some branches fuse at their bases, creating a multi-stemmed appearance in older or larger specimens.
Color:
•          Predominantly golden-yellow to mustard-yellow throughout the branches, with occasional slight variations depending on lighting and individual specimen age.
•          The base and lower branches often display darker tan, olive-brown, or greenish tones, particularly in the basal 5 to 10 cm of the colony.
•          Upper branches are typically brighter yellow, with tips sometimes appearing slightly paler or more translucent than the main branch body.
•          Oscule rims are occasionally orange or tan, creating subtle visual punctuation against the yellow branches.
•          No bicoloration pattern (unlike Form B of A. crassa) is present; the color transitions are gradual, not abrupt.
•          The colour appears consistent across different lighting angles and depths.
Surface features:
•          The branch surface is smooth to slightly uneven, less obviously convoluted than A. cauliformis.
•          Oscules are very small (0.3 to 1 mm in diameter), densely distributed along the length of branches, arranged in roughly linear or helical rows running parallel to the branch axis.
•          Oscule rims are minimally raised, appearing as fine dark lines or dots rather than prominent collars.
•          The surface between oscules is smooth or slightly bumpy, with no obvious ridges or fluting except occasionally fine radial striations emanating from the branch axis.
•          Close-ups reveal a fine, slightly granular texture overall; the surface is matte rather than glossy.
•          No fistules, constrictions, or lateral branches emerge perpendicularly from the main branches.
Visual context clues:
•          Frequently photographed with small fish (wrasses, gobies, other reef fish) hovering among branches, attracted to the protected space.
•          Often surrounded by coralline algae, coral polyps, and tunicates growing on adjacent substrate.
•          The upright, delicate branching pattern creates a distinctive silhouette against the reef profile, easily recognized in wide-angle reef photos.
•          Yellow colour stands out well against dark rock or coral, but blends more with sand or lighter substrate.
•          Sometimes partially shaded or obscured by larger sponges or coral heads in dense reef areas, but the exposed upper branches are always visible.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The upright, evenly branching yellow form distinguishes A. fulva clearly from Aplysina fistularis (which has taller, more columnar main stems with stochastic sub-branching) and from Aplysina archeri (which is more tangled and less regularly organized).
•          The slender, wiry branches contrast with Form B of Aiolochroia crassa (which is thicker, more rigidly parallel, and distinctly bicoloured).
•          Differs from Aiolochroia crassa Form A by being more delicate, more consistently yellow, and less massive.
-----

species.name: Cliona delitrix
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A bright red to reddish-orange sponge that forms thin, encrusting patches tightly adhered to hard surfaces. It often spreads in irregular shapes across coral colonies and surrounding substrate, sometimes forming clusters of small patches or expanding into larger continuous mats. The sponge usually looks like it is breaking through or erupting from coral tissue, creating bold red areas surrounded by pale coral skeleton.
Growth Form & Shape
Always encrusting: it hugs the surface and does not form thick lobes, fingers, or upright tubes.
appears as patches or blotches that are uneven in shape — circular, elongated, or irregular.
Patches can occur individually or merge together into larger irregular areas as they spread.
Often seen emerging from holes, crevices, or breaks in coral tissue, giving the impression of “breaking through” the coral surface.
Color
Typically bright red, orange-red, or brick red — often among the most vivid colors on the reef.
Color is solid and uniform across each patch.
May appear slightly darker or browner in shaded areas or when covered by a thin film of sediment, but still retains its distinctive reddish tone.
Surface and Texture
Surface is flat to gently uneven but always closely attached to the substrate.
The most obvious and distinctive feature is the presence of large, round exhalent openings (oscules).
These oscules are prominent and easy to see — usually 2–10 mm wide and scattered across the sponge surface.
Each opening often has a slightly raised, smooth rim that may appear lighter in color.
From above, they look like small, neat holes or short tunnels punctuating the red surface.
Visual Context Clues
Most often found on living coral colonies, particularly massive species.
Bright red patches are typically surrounded by pale coral skeleton or live coral tissue, creating a stark color contrast.
Often seen penetrating through coral tissue, producing clusters of oscules within otherwise intact coral heads.
In many cases, areas of dead or dying coral tissue border the sponge patches, suggesting overgrowth.
Diagnostic Look in Photos
Bright red encrusting patches with large, conspicuous round holes scattered across them.
Growth often appears irregular, patchy, or invasive, with sponge visible in cracks, breaks, or holes in coral.
A strong visual cue is the contrast between vivid red sponge tissue and pale coral skeleton or living tissue around it.

species.name: Mycale laevis
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A thin, bright orange to yellow-orange sponge that forms flat, spreading crusts over the reef surface. It usually appears as a thin band or patch wrapping around the base or underside of hard corals. The sponge has an irregular edge that follows the contours of whatever it is growing on, often looking like melted icing spilling outward.
Growth form:
Always encrusting and closely attached to the surface beneath it — never raised into tubes or lobes.
Usually found right up against coral tissue or skeleton, often peeking out beneath dome- or plate-shaped corals.
Visible portions can range from narrow, winding bands to wide, spreading sheets.
Color:
Bright orange to yellow-orange and often the most striking feature in the image.
Color is uniform across the surface but can vary slightly in saturation from area to area.
Surface texture (visible only):
Appears rough and granular, as if sprinkled with fine crumbs.
The surface is uneven but mostly flat, without pronounced ridges or projections.
Oscules (exhalent pores):
Several large, round holes scattered across the surface.
These are usually much bigger and more obvious than the pores of other sponges, and are often ringed by a slightly raised rim.
Some oscules are large enough to look like short tunnels or little chimneys, visible even in distant photos.
Context clues in images:
Most often visible at the edge of living coral, especially on the undersides or where the coral grows outward.
The sponge may form a thin bright orange band that sharply contrasts with the pale coral skeleton or surrounding rock.
Sometimes seen tucked under an overhang or ledge, glowing orange in shaded areas.

species.name: Callyspongia plicifera
species.description:
Visual Description
Overall Form and Shape
Callyspongia plicifera is usually found as a single large vase rising from the substrate, but it can sometimes occur in clusters of two or three. The vase is tubular or trumpet-like, often tapering toward the base and flaring widely at the top. The overall shape is rigid and upright, and the sponge usually grows vertically from a single point of attachment.
Surface Texture and Structure
The surface is one of its most distinctive features. It is heavily ridged and folded, forming a series of deep valleys and raised ridges that run vertically along the sides and around the opening. These folds can look like wrinkled fabric or carved channels. The inner surface of the vase is often smooth or slightly textured, contrasting with the deeply sculpted outer wall.
Color and Appearance Underwater
This species is often a translucent pale blue, violet, or white, though pinkish or lavender tones are also common. The surface often looks as though it is glowing or fluorescing underwater, especially under natural sunlight — this is a real field clue. Its surface is also very reflective, which can make it tricky to photograph. The inner wall of the vase is often slightly lighter in color than the exterior.
Size and Growth Pattern
Individual vases are typically 30–60 cm tall and 15–30 cm wide at the opening, though some may exceed this. They are usually stiff-walled and maintain their form even in moderate currents. Multiple vases, when present, may grow very close together but still remain distinctly separate tubes rather than fusing into a mass.
Other Features to Note in the Field
The opening (osculum) is usually wide and circular to oval, often tilted or flared.
The rim of the vase is frequently irregular or wavy, with a slightly frilled appearance.
The inside of the osculum may show a delicate network of small holes or fine texture.
The sponge is often found in exposed, well-lit reef areas, attached to hard substrate or coral heads.

species.name: Aiolochroia crassa
species.description:
Aiolochroia crassa visual identification description
Visual description
Overall appearance:
Aiolochroia crassa appears as a chunky, irregular, raised sponge with thick lobes, short tubes, or fused mound-like branches. Its strongest visible cues are a rough knobby surface, rounded lobes or tube-like projections, and large circular oscula that often show striking yellow internal tissue. In images, it may look like a lumpy purple, yellow, tan, or mixed-color sponge with crater-like openings.
Growth form:
The body is usually massive, lobate, or branching-tubular. It often forms thick, blunt lobes or short chimney-like projections that may be fused together at the base. The overall shape is irregular rather than cleanly cylindrical. It should read as bulky and thick-walled, not thin, rope-like, delicate, or flat. Some individuals appear as a mound with several raised lobes; others look more like a cluster of fat tubes.
Color:
External color is variable. It may appear purple, lavender, brownish-purple, yellow, orange-yellow, tan, greenish, blue-gray, or mixed purple and yellow. A key visible feature is the bright lemon-yellow to golden-yellow color inside the oscula. This yellow may appear as an inner wall, rim, patch, or septa-like internal partition visible through the opening. In some images, the exterior may be muted, but the inside of the oscula remains sharply yellow and visually distinctive.
Surface features:
The surface is coarse, knobby, and uneven. It often appears warty, pebbled, blistered, or conulose rather than smooth. The bumps are rounded and irregular, creating a rough texture across the lobes. Oscula are usually round to oval and may appear as dark holes with yellow internal walls or yellow-rimmed interiors. The openings are often placed on the tops or upper surfaces of lobes.
Top-down view:
From above, Aiolochroia crassa may not look obviously like a branching tube sponge. It often appears as an irregular raised mound or fused cluster of lobes with several round crater-like openings. The best top-down cues are: rough knobby texture, uneven lobed outline, visible surface relief, and circular oscula with bright yellow interiors. In photoquadrats or orthomosaics, it may read as a lumpy purple/yellow/tan patch with dark circular holes and yellow inner walls. Without a side view, the tube structure may be partly hidden, so the oscula and knobby surface become more important than branch shape.
Visual context clues:
It usually appears attached to hard reef structure rather than lying as a loose object. It may project above nearby benthos and cast small shadows, especially when lobes are upright. It can be partly surrounded by algae, coral, rubble, or other sponges, but the useful annotation cues are its raised, chunky relief and bright yellow oscular interiors.
Distinguishing from similar Caribbean sponge genera
Versus Aplysina:
Aplysina can also be yellow, purple, or branching, so it is a likely visual confusion. Aplysina often appears more rope-like, finger-like, or regularly tubular, with smoother or more evenly reticulated surfaces. Aiolochroia crassa is usually chunkier, more fused, more mound-like, and more irregular, with round oscula that often reveal vivid yellow internal tissue.
Versus Niphates:
Niphates often forms smoother tubes, branches, or vase-like shapes with cleaner outlines. In images it tends to look more evenly cylindrical or neatly tubular. Aiolochroia crassa is rougher, heavier, more knobby, and less regular, with blunt lobes and crater-like oscula rather than clean tube openings.
Versus Iotrochota:
Iotrochota is often purple or dark violet and may appear branching, ropey, bushy, or irregularly encrusting. It is usually thinner and more wiry or sheet-like than Aiolochroia crassa. Aiolochroia crassa has thicker lobes, a bulkier raised body, more obvious round oscula, and yellow internal color visible inside openings.
Versus Agelas:
Agelas tube sponges may form orange, brown, or reddish clusters of tubes. They often appear more pipe-like, cylindrical, or vase-like, with more uniform tube walls. Aiolochroia crassa tends to look more fused, lumpy, and conulose, with a rougher surface and often a stronger yellow interior visible in the oscula.
Versus Smenospongia:
Smenospongia can be massive, lobed, dark, or encrusting and may have visible oscula. It usually appears darker, smoother, or more cushion-like, without the same bright yellow oscular interiors. Aiolochroia crassa should show a more conspicuous combination of chunky lobes, knobby surface texture, and yellow internal tissue.
Versus Ircinia:
Ircinia species often appear as brown, tan, gray, or dark cushion-like masses, lobes, or encrusting forms. They can be bumpy, but they usually look more fibrous, drab, or cushiony. Aiolochroia crassa is more likely to show thick branching or lobed projections, round crater-like oscula, and vivid yellow visible inside the openings.
Versus Callyspongia:
Callyspongia often appears as cleaner tubes or vases with smoother walls and more regular openings. It may look more delicate, open, or cup-like. Aiolochroia crassa is rougher, chunkier, more irregular, and more mound-like, with a strongly knobby surface and yellow oscular interiors.
Annotation shorthand
A chunky, raised, knobby sponge with thick fused lobes or short tubes and round crater-like oscula. External color is variable, but the oscula often show bright lemon-yellow to golden-yellow internal walls or septa-like tissue. From above, look for a lumpy purple/yellow/tan mound with rough surface relief and circular holes; do not rely on color alone.

species.name: Amphimedon nodosa
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance
A tall, slender, erect rope-like sponge that appears as one or several dark reddish-brown to maroon vertical rods rising from the reef. The sponge is usually narrow, firm-looking, and relatively uniform in width, with a smooth but finely roughened surface. In many images it looks like a dark red-brown cord, strap, or flattened rope rather than a true hollow tube. Individuals may appear as a single upright stem, but more often show a small cluster of sparsely branching upright stems emerging from a shared base.
The most distinctive visual impression is a dark, vertical, compressed sponge with a rigid, rope-like form. It does not form a bushy tree, a tangled cluster, or a wide fan. It usually occupies a narrow three-dimensional space, with only a few stems or branches visible.
Growth form
Develops from a firm attachment point on rock, rubble, dead coral, or hard substrate.
Usually grows as one to several upright stems arising from a shared or closely grouped base.
Stems are slender, elongated, and rope-like, often straight to gently curved.
Branching is sparse and irregular. When branches are present, they are usually few, upright, and similar in thickness to the main stem.
The sponge may appear unbranched in single-frame images, especially if only one stem is visible.
Stems are often laterally compressed, giving them a flattened, strap-like, blade-like, or oval cross-section rather than a perfectly round tube.
Diameter or visible width is usually narrow relative to height, commonly around 1 to 3 cm.
Height can range from short upright rods to tall stems several tens of centimeters high, sometimes approaching or exceeding 1 m.
Tips are rounded, blunt, or softly tapered, not sharply pointed.
The form is more rigid and vertical than tangled or flexible-looking.
Color
Predominantly dark reddish-brown, burgundy, maroon, wine-red, or dark purple-brown.
Some individuals appear more brown-red or rusty red depending on lighting, depth, and camera color balance.
Lower portions may appear darker, sometimes nearly blackish brown or deep purple-brown.
Upper portions and tips may appear slightly lighter, redder, or more orange-brown.
Color transitions are gradual, not sharply banded.
No strong yellow, green, or blue coloration is expected.
No obvious bicolored exterior pattern is present.
Damaged or shaded areas may appear darker than the exposed outer surface.
Surface features
Surface appears matte, roughened, finely granular, or sandpapery.
Texture is usually visible as fine speckling, small pores, or tiny raised granules across the stem.
Small openings may be scattered along the surface, but they are not usually large, flared, or visually dominant.
Oscules, when visible, appear as small dark pits or slightly lighter-rimmed openings.
The surface does not show large tube mouths at the tips.
The surface lacks strong longitudinal ridges, deep grooves, fluting, or obvious corrugation.
No fistules or conspicuous side tubes are present.
Older individuals may show small irregular bumps, epibionts, sediment, or abrasion marks, but the main surface remains rope-like and compressed.
Top-down image appearance
From a top-down or oblique reef image, Amphimedon nodosa may appear as a dark reddish-brown line, rod, or narrow strap crossing the frame or rising diagonally from the substrate. Because the sponge is tall and narrow, top-down imagery may foreshorten it, making it look like a short dark oval, flattened bar, or curved red-brown strip rather than a tall vertical stem.
The compressed cross-section is especially important in top-down views. Instead of a round yellow tube or branching tree, the sponge may show a flattened, blade-like profile with a dark maroon surface and fine granular texture. If several stems are present, they usually appear as a small number of separated, upright dark rods rather than a dense bush.
Visual context clues
Often stands out as a dark red-brown vertical or diagonal element against paler sand, rubble, or reef pavement.
May be partly hidden among corals, algae, gorgonians, or other sponges, but the exposed portions remain narrow and rope-like.
Does not usually create much sheltering space for fish because it is sparsely branched.
In low light or bluish underwater imagery, the sponge may appear very dark brown, nearly black, or muted purple-brown.
The vertical silhouette may remain more visible than the red coloration when color correction is poor.
Nearby fish, coral heads, or diver features often emphasize how narrow the sponge is relative to its height.
Diagnostic look in photos
Best recognized by the combination of dark red-brown to maroon color, erect rope-like growth, sparse branching, and compressed or flattened stems.
Differs from Aplysina fulva by being dark red-brown rather than yellow and by lacking a delicate tree-like branching pattern.
Differs from Aplysina fistularis by being darker, narrower, more compressed, and not forming conspicuous yellow tube clusters with large terminal openings.
Differs from Aiolochroia crassa by being much narrower, more rope-like, less massive, and not bicolored or thickly lobed.
Differs from Ptilocaulis walpersi by usually appearing darker, smoother, more compressed, and less obviously prickly or highly branched.
Differs from Niphates species by its firmer-looking, compressed red-brown rope form rather than softer, more irregular tubular or branching forms.
Differs from Agelas tube sponges by lacking large open tube mouths and by presenting as a narrow compressed rod or strap rather than a vase-like or clustered tubular sponge.
-----

species.name: Xestospongia muta
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A massive, typically barrel or vase-shaped sponge that is amongst the largest sponges in the Caribbean, often reaching 1 to 2 meters or more in height. The exterior is characteristically reddish-brown, tan, salmon, or brick-red in colour, with a very distinctive large, prominent central opening at the top (the osculum) that is often visibly pink, purple, or burgundy inside. The overall form is thick-walled and sturdy, with a smooth to slightly bumpy exterior covered with thousands of tiny pores (ostia). The sponge typically grows upright from a solid base, dominating its local reef space, and can be recognized from a distance by its size and colour alone.
Growth form:
•          Develops from a broad, massive base (often 0.5 to 1 m in width) that firmly anchors the sponge to rock or coral rubble.
•          The main body expands upward in a roughly barrel or cylindrical shape, sometimes slightly compressed or flattened on one side.
•          The walls are extremely thick (8 to 20 cm or more), making the sponge very heavy and structurally robust.
•          The upper opening (osculum) is large and prominent, typically 10 to 30 cm in diameter, with a faintly raised or rolled rim.
•          Some specimens develop multiple oscules or lateral openings, but a single large dorsal osculum is most common.
•          The exterior is generally smooth, without prominent lobes, branches, or fistules, though some bumpy or irregular growth can occur on older individuals.
•          Smaller juveniles may be more conical or cone-shaped before developing the classic barrel form.
•          Maximum height typically 0.5 to 2 m, with proportional width.
Color:
•          Exterior is predominantly reddish-brown, tan-brown, salmon, or brick-red, with considerable variation between individual specimens.
•          Some specimens are darker mahogany or almost purple-brown, while others are paler tan or peachy.
•          The interior walls and rim of the osculum are visibly darker (deep burgundy, maroon, or purplish-brown).
•          The interior flesh is deep red, maroon, or purple, creating strong visual contrast with the paler exterior.
•          No patterns (stripes, spots, or mottling) are typically present; the colour is relatively uniform across the exterior.
•          Color can appear darker or lighter depending on lighting angle and water clarity.
Surface features:
•          The exterior surface is smooth overall but covered with innumerable tiny ostia (inhalant pores), each 0.1 to 0.5 mm in diameter, giving the surface a finely pitted or pebbly appearance.
•          Ostia are uniformly distributed across the entire exterior.
•          The osculum rim is smooth or slightly convoluted, with the interior walls showing faint ridges or lamellae visible looking into the opening.
•          Some older specimens show irregular bumps, growths, or encrusted areas where other organisms have colonized the surface.
•          The exterior surface is matte or slightly dull, never shiny or translucent.
•          No obvious fistules are present on healthy individuals.
Visual context clues:
•          Stands out dramatically on the reef by its sheer size alone, often towering above surrounding coral and other sponges.
•          Frequently hosts small fish (gobies, wrasses, blennies) that hover in or near the osculum for shelter.
•          The large opening and internal space often contain small crustaceans, molluscs, and other cryptic fauna.
•          Surrounded by a halo of current (sediment disturbance) visible in high-current areas, indicating the strong water flow through the sponge.
•          Often partially encrusted or overgrown by coral polyps, hydroids, or other sessile organisms on older individuals.
•          The orange-brown to red colour contrasts distinctly with green coral or blue water, making it visible from a significant distance.
•          Scale references from divers clearly show the massive size, often larger than a human torso in height.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The massive size, barrel-like shape, large apical osculum, and reddish-brown colour make X. muta unmistakable and instantly recognizable in the field.
•          Readily distinguished from other large Caribbean sponges like Geodia (which are more spherical and lighter coloured) and Cliona spp. (which are smaller and more encrusting).
•          The large central opening is the key diagnostic feature and is never observed in Aiolochroia or Aplysina species.
-----

species.name: Agelas clathrodes
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A massive, encrusting to lobate sponge with a distinctive bright orange to red-orange exterior and a lighter interior, presenting large, flabby lobes or flattened plates that often merge together. The sponge grows in thick, undulating sheets or forms prominent rounded protrusions across available substrate, sometimes resembling enlarged elephant ears. The surface appears slightly wrinkled or verrucose, giving a textured appearance even at distance. Growth patterns are irregular and asymmetrical, with lobes spreading widely across rock or coral surfaces and occasionally bridging gaps between substrates.
Growth form:
•          The sponge develops as thick, flattened lobes or ear-like projections that are typically wider than they are tall, often reaching 10 centimetres or more in thickness.
•          Individual lobes fuse together seamlessly, creating a continuous surface rather than distinct, separate branches, resulting in a unified mass appearance.
•          Lobe edges curl or roll slightly outward, particularly at the apices, creating a characteristic scalloped or wavy margin visible in profile.
•          The base attaches broadly to hard substrate without stalks or prominent attachment points, allowing rapid lateral expansion across available surface.
•          Growth is predominantly horizontal and spreading rather than erect, with colonies sometimes covering more than a metre of reef substrate.
•          Multiple lobes often interlock or overlap, creating a folded or compressed appearance when viewed from above.
Color:
•          Exterior is bright orange, red-orange, or sometimes orange-yellow, presenting a vivid, uniform color that remains consistent across colonies.
•          Interior is noticeably lighter, ranging from cream to pale orange, visible when the sponge is sectioned or partially damaged.
•          Color remains relatively stable across different lighting conditions, though deeper shadows within recesses appear slightly more reddish-brown.
•          In deep-water specimens, color may shift slightly toward more brownish-orange tones, but orange predominates at typical reef depths.
•          No significant color variation across seasons or between individual specimens has been documented.
Surface features:
•          The surface is slightly rough or verrucose, with fine wrinkles and corrugations running across the tissue, visible especially in close-up photographs.
•          Abundant round to slightly oval oscules are scattered across the entire surface, each approximately 0.2 to 0.5 centimetres in diameter, appearing as distinct dark openings.
•          Oscules are often arranged in loose, curving rows or chains that follow the surface topography, rather than random distribution.
•          Each oscule typically has a thin, slightly raised rim that may be slightly paler or translucent compared to surrounding tissue.
•          Smaller incurrent pores (ostia) are distributed densely across the surface but are only clearly visible in extreme close-up or microscopy.
•          The texture becomes noticeably rougher and more prominent in response to sedimentation or nutrient-rich conditions, with increased verrucosity observed.
Visual context clues:
•          Often surrounded by diverse companion organisms; algae, small corals, and other sponges frequently colonize nearby substrate and sometimes establish on the sponge surface itself.
•          Frequently positioned on vertical reef walls or the sides of large coral heads, where water current is strong and sediment load is lower.
•          The sponge often sits flush against hard substrate with no visible gap, indicating strong adhesion and long-term establishment.
•          In photographs, dramatic lighting from the side highlights the thickness and relief of the lobes, creating pronounced shadows that emphasize the ear-like structure.
•          Occasional small fish and crustaceans visible near oscules, attracted to the current generated by water expulsion.
•          Easily distinguished from Agelas conifera by its uniformly flattened, plate-like form rather than conical or club-shaped projections.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The bright, uniform orange-red color with large flattened lobes immediately distinguishes A. clathrodes from the tan to brown A. conifera.
•          Unlike Aplysina tube sponges, A. clathrodes shows no tubular or cylindrical structures; it is entirely encrusting to massive lobate without any distinct tubelike outgrowths.
•          The densely scattered oscules visible on the surface at moderate magnification readily differentiate it from other Caribbean Agelas species that may have fewer, more clustered oscules.
•          The thick, flabby lobes with wrinkled surfaces are distinctive compared to firmer, more regularly-shaped growth forms of other species.
-----

species.name: Agelas conifera
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A medium to large sponge with distinctive brown, tan, or greyish-brown coloration that exhibits highly variable growth forms including cones, clubs, antlers, octopus-like branches, or ridge-shaped projections depending on geographic location and local environmental conditions. The sponge grows in erect to semi-erect posture, with multiple projections or cones arising from a shared base or spreading point. Larger specimens form complex three-dimensional structures where cones overlap or cluster together, creating a densely branched appearance. The surface is firm and relatively smooth compared to the verrucose textures of other Agelas species.
Growth form:
•          Cone-shaped or conical projections predominate, with individual cones wider at the base and tapering slightly toward the apex, typically ranging from 5 to 15 centimetres in height.
•          Multiple cones arise from a common base or basal platform, creating a clustered or tufted appearance; in some colonies, cones number in the dozens.
•          In geographic variants, forms include the octopus form (long, dangling branches), the club form (short, erect cones with bulbous tips), and the antler form (branching projections extending upward and outward).
•          Basal attachment is broad and solid, with the sponge firmly anchored to rock or coral substrate without stalks between the base and individual cones.
•          Individual projections are cylindrical to gently tapered, with a characteristic nipple-like osculum visible at the apex of each cone.
•          Smaller specimens may possess single tall cones or multiple shorter cones, while larger colonies integrate into massive structures with complex branching patterns.
Color:
•          Exterior is consistently brown, tan, brownish-grey, or occasionally greyish-brown, with a relatively uniform tone across the sponge.
•          Interior tissue is notably lighter, ranging from cream to pale tan, visible in broken regions or at lobe margins.
•          Color shows no striking patterning and remains even across the surface except where sediment accumulation or algal growth may create transient markings.
•          Lighter yellowish tints may appear in sunlit shallow-water specimens, while deeper populations tend toward more saturated brown tones.
•          No significant seasonal or temporal color variation has been documented in this species.
Surface features:
•          The surface is relatively smooth and firm, lacking the prominent wrinkling seen in A. clathrodes.
•          A single, prominent large osculum is visible at the apex of each cone, typically circular or slightly oval, approximately 0.3 to 0.7 centimetres in diameter.
•          The osculum is surrounded by a slightly raised or thickened rim that may be slightly paler in color and appears distinctly demarcated from surrounding tissue.
•          Smaller incurrent ostia are scattered across the body surface in a distributed pattern, visible only in magnified photographs.
•          The overall surface texture is finely granulate or smooth, occasionally appearing slightly sticky or glistening due to mucus layers.
•          In areas with high sedimentation, the sponge surface may appear duller and less glossy due to accumulated fine particles.
Visual context clues:
•          Often found on outer reef slopes and vertical walls where current is strong, frequently growing alongside corals of the families Acroporidae and Poaceae.
•          Frequently positioned in groups of multiple individuals, sometimes densely packed, creating forests of cones across large reef sections.
•          The sponge often hosts small crustaceans and fish that shelter within the spaces between cones or near oscules.
•          In underwater photographs, the stacked or clustered cone arrangement creates a distinctive silhouette even at distance.
•          Geographic morphotype variations are highly visible in collection photographs; Venezuelan specimens show octopus forms, Bahamian specimens show antler forms, and Belizean specimens show club forms.
•          Readily distinguished from A. clathrodes by the presence of multiple erect cones or clubs rather than flattened lobes, and from Aplysina species by the solid sponge body without tubular cavities.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The distinctive cone, club, or antler-shaped erect projections immediately identify this species compared to the uniformly flattened, ear-like lobes of A. clathrodes.
•          The brown to tan coloration contrasts sharply with the bright orange-red of A. clathrodes and with the pink, purple, or yellow hues of Aplysina species.
•          The single osculum per cone apex is readily visible and distinctly different from the scattered oscules across the body of other Agelas species.
•          Unlike Aplysina tube sponges, A. conifera shows no hollow interior or open tubular structure; the sponge body is dense and solid.
-----

species.name: Aplysina archeri
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A distinctive tube sponge characterized by long, slender cylindrical tubes of uniform diameter, typically ranging in colour from lavender, pink, grey, brown, or reddish tones, depending on individual and population variation. The sponge grows as one to many tubes arising from a shared basal platform, often forming large clusters of up to 22 or more tubes that extend vertically or semi-vertically into the water column. Tubes are typically smooth-walled and featureless except for the osculum, creating a clean, orderly appearance. Individual colonies may occupy a substantial area of reef space and are often conspicuous from a distance due to their height and clustered arrangement.
Growth form:
•          Cylindrical tubes are the primary growth form, typically 2 to 6 feet (60 centimetres to 1.8 metres) in height in healthy mature specimens, with a remarkably uniform diameter from base to apex.
•          Tubes are hollow and internally open, creating a distinctive tube-like morphology absent in the Agelas genus; the interior is continuous from base to apex.
•          Multiple tubes arise from a shared, expanded base or basal platform that may be flattened or mound-like; the base is firmly attached to hard substrate.
•          Tubes are relatively rigid and self-supporting, maintaining an erect to semi-erect posture without lateral sprawling or drooping.
•          Individual tubes remain largely independent, though occasional lateral fusion or bridging may occur between adjacent tubes in densely-packed colonies.
•          Tips are blunt and rounded at the osculum, with each tube apex typically terminating in a well-defined oscule opening.
Color:
•          Coloration is highly variable among individuals and populations, including lavender, pink, purple, pale grey, brown, tan, or combinations thereof.
•          Color is typically uniform along the entire length of each tube, with little gradient from base to apex.
•          Interior tissue is distinctly paler than the exterior, appearing cream, pale lavender, or pale pink; visible at the osculum and in sectioned specimens.
•          Some specimens show subtle banding or mottling, particularly in pink or purple tones, creating minor textural visual interest.
•          Colour remains relatively stable across different lighting angles, though shadows in the tube opening may appear darker due to the depth of the osculum.
•          In some populations, reddish or brownish tones predominate, suggesting geographic variation in pigmentation.
Surface features:
•          The exterior surface is smooth and featureless, lacking the verrucosity or wrinkling seen in encrusting Agelas species.
•          A single, large, prominent osculum is positioned at the apex of each tube, typically approximately 0.5 to 1 centimetre in diameter.
•          The osculum opening is typically slightly flared or expanded at the rim, with edges that may be slightly raised or thickened.
•          Incurrent pores (ostia) are distributed across the tube surface but are microscopic and invisible in standard photographs; the tube exterior appears featureless.
•          The surface has a slightly matte or satiny appearance, occasionally with visible mucus layers that provide a subtle sheen.
•          Close examination reveals a finely microvillous or corrugated texture at extreme magnification, though imperceptible to the naked eye.
Visual context clues:
•          Typically found on outer reef slopes, drop-offs, and vertical walls, often positioned in areas of strong and consistent current.
•          Frequently occurs in groups or clusters, with multiple individuals positioned adjacently, creating a “forest” effect.
•          Often surrounded by gorgonians, stony corals, and other sponges, establishing dense sponge gardens in appropriate habitats.
•          The tall, cylindrical form with prominent oscule openings creates distinctive visual features even in wide-angle reef photographs.
•          Schools of fish often hover near clusters, attracted to the current generated by oscular water expulsion.
•          Readily distinguished from A. fistularis by the typically lavender, pink, or grey coloration (vs. yellow-orange in A. fistularis) and by the frequent presence of multiple tubes in large clusters rather than typically solitary or paired tubes.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The lavender, pink, or grey coloration distinguishes A. archeri from the typically bright yellow-orange of A. fistularis and the yellow or brown tones of A. insularis.
•          The smooth, cylindrical tube form without any finger-like projections or surface roughening contrasts clearly with A. insularis, which displays prominent finger-like projections.
•          The uniform diameter along the tube length and the large, singular osculum per tube are distinctive features compared to other Aplysina species.
•          Unlike encrusting Agelas species, A. archeri shows no flattened lobes or conical projections; it is distinctly tubular and erect.
-----

species.name: Aplysina fistularis
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A striking bright yellow to ochre-coloured tube sponge, among the most visually distinctive Caribbean reef sponges, forming thick-walled cylindrical tubes of substantial diameter that typically grow in solitary or paired configurations. Individual tubes are remarkably robust and inflated, with high, rigid walls that give a distinctive barrel-like or stovepipe appearance. The sponge is often conspicuous on reefs due to its vivid yellow coloration, which may shift toward ochre or golden-tan in deeper water or areas with reduced light penetration. Larger specimens are visually dominant despite their relatively small colony size, owing to the massive diameter of the tubes.
Growth form:
•          Single large tube or multiple paired tubes arising from a shared, closed base that is sessile (immobile) and firmly attached to hard substrate.
•          Tubes are thick-walled, rigid, and self-supporting, with an open, hollow interior that extends the entire length from base to apex.
•          Individual tubes are typically 50 centimetres or less in height in clear water, but may reach up to 1 metre or more in high-sedimentation reef zones where reduced light is compensated by increased water flow.
•          Tube diameter is substantial and uniform, typically ranging from 5 to 15 centimetres, creating a distinctive barrel or stovepipe silhouette.
•          Multiple tubes, when present, remain largely independent without significant lateral fusion, though occasional bridging or contact occurs.
•          The closed basal platform is often broad and flattened, occasionally showing slight mounding or ridge-like elevation above the substrate.
Color:
•          Exterior is bright yellow, ochre-yellow, or golden-yellow, providing a striking visual contrast with surrounding reef elements.
•          Colour is uniform across the tube surface, with little gradient from base to apex in healthy specimens.
•          Interior tissue is noticeably paler, appearing cream or pale yellow; visible when viewing the osculum opening or in sectioned material.
•          In deep water below 30 metres, fluorescence under reduced blue light causes the sponge to appear intensely glowing or lime-green, a distinctive adaptation visible in deep-water photography.
•          No significant seasonal variation in colour has been documented.
•          Minor surface accumulation of sediment may create a slightly duller, brownish cast on otherwise bright yellow specimens, but the underlying yellow is always apparent.
Surface features:
•          The exterior surface is smooth, firm, and featureless, entirely lacking verrucosity or prominent textural features.
•          A single, very large, prominent osculum is positioned at the apex, typically 0.5 to 1.5 centimetres in diameter, representing one of the largest oscule openings of any Caribbean sponge.
•          The osculum opening is typically slightly flared or funnel-shaped, with edges that may be slightly raised or slightly incurled.
•          Thin, transparent ridged internal walls are visible within and immediately below the osculum opening, representing the internal skeletal structure.
•          Incurrent pores (ostia) are microscopically small and scattered across the body surface but are invisible in standard underwater photography.
•          The surface has a finely granulate or satiny appearance, occasionally appearing slightly glistening due to mucus layers.
Visual context clues:
•          Typically found on coral and rocky reefs in areas of strong, sustained current, preferring locations where water flow remains consistent.
•          Often positioned on vertical reef walls, outer slopes, and drop-offs, where current is maximized and sediment settlement minimized.
•          Frequently surrounded by gorgonians and sea fans that similarly favour high-current environments.
•          The vivid yellow coloration makes this sponge extremely conspicuous in wide-angle reef photographs, even when partially obscured by other reef elements.
•          Small fish and crustaceans sometimes hover near the osculum, attracted to the feeding current.
•          Readily distinguished from A. archeri by the bright yellow coloration (vs. lavender, pink, or grey in A. archeri) and by the typically solitary or paired tube form rather than large clusters.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The bright yellow, ochre, or golden coloration is instantly distinctive among Caribbean sponges and easily separates A. fistularis from all other Aplysina species.
•          The smooth tube without finger-like projections or surface roughness contrasts with A. insularis, which displays prominent digitate (finger-like) projections.
•          The typically solitary or paired tube form with minimal clustering distinguishes it from A. archeri, which commonly forms large clusters of many tubes.
•          The thick, inflated tube walls and large osculum are visually distinctive features compared to other sponge genera.
-----

species.name: Aplysina insularis
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A yellow to yellowish-brown tube sponge with a distinctive and highly characteristic feature set of finger-like projections or slender tendrils arising from the main tube body, creating a complex, ornate silhouette. The sponge typically exhibits multiple tubes per colony, ranging from approximately 2 to 7 tubes in shallow populations to 3 to 4 tubes in deeper populations, with considerable variation in tube abundance based on depth and environmental conditions. The predominant growth form is tubular, but the distinctive digitate (finger-like) outgrowths from tube apices or flanks create a visually ornate structure unlike any other Caribbean Aplysina species. Colonies may appear delicate despite possessing solid, robust tube walls.
Growth form:
•          Multiple tubes (typically 2 to 7 per colony) arising from a shared basal platform that is broad and firmly attached to hard substrate.
•          Individual tubes are cylindrical and of relatively uniform diameter (typically 1 to 4 centimetres), with an open, hollow interior extending from base to apex.
•          Prominent finger-like projections or tendrils emanate from the tube apex or from the flanks of the main tubes; these projections are distinctly narrower than the main tube and taper toward blunt or slightly expanded tips.
•          The digitate projections are typically 5 to 15 millimetres in diameter and may extend 2 to 10 centimetres from the main tube.
•          In high-sedimentation environments, these rope-like and tendril projections may actually exceed the main tube in size and prominence, creating an unusual morphology.
•          Individual tubes remain largely independent but may show occasional lateral contact or minor fusion.
•          Tube height varies significantly with depth: shallow-water specimens typically possess shorter tubes (15 to 25 centimetres) with more numerous projections, while deeper specimens (30 to 40 metres) exhibit longer tubes (50 centimetres or more) with fewer but more prominent projections.
Color:
•          Exterior is yellowish-brown, ochre-brown, or warm brown, with yellow tones predominating in shallow water.
•          Interior tissue is paler, appearing cream or pale yellow; visible at osculum openings and in sectioned specimens.
•          In deeper water below 25 metres, the sponge exhibits intense green-yellow fluorescence under blue light conditions, an adaptation attributed to fluorescent pigments concentrated in surface tissue.
•          Colour is relatively uniform across individual tubes, though slight variation among tubes within a single colony may occur.
•          No prominent patterning or mottling is present, though minor surface accumulation of sediment may create transient markings.
•          Color may appear slightly duller or more brownish in high-sediment environments compared to clear-water populations.
Surface features:
•          The main tube exterior is smooth and featureless, lacking the verrucosity or roughness of encrusting species.
•          One or more prominent oscula are positioned at the apex of each main tube, typically 0.5 to 1 centimetre in diameter.
•          The osculum is typically surrounded by a slightly raised or thickened rim and often shows gentle flaring or funnel-like shaping at the opening margin.
•          Osculum rims are often slightly paler than surrounding tube tissue, creating a subtle contrasting band.
•          Finger-like projections possess the same smooth surface as the main tube body, though their tapering form may create subtle shading.
•          Incurrent pores (ostia) are microscopically small and distributed across the body surface but are invisible in standard photography.
•          A finely granulate or satiny surface finish is typical, with occasional visible mucus layers providing subtle sheen.
Visual context clues:
•          Found on outer reef slopes and vertical walls, particularly in moderately deep water ranging from 15 to 40 metres, though occasionally in shallower areas.
•          Frequently occurs in areas with moderate to strong current and elevated sedimentation loads.
•          The distinctive finger-like projections create immediately recognizable visual features even in wide-angle colony photographs.
•          Often surrounded by other sponges, gorgonians, and soft corals, establishing dense communities on suitable reef substrates.
•          Depth-dependent morphological variation is visually apparent: photographs from similar depths within a region show consistent projection abundance and tube morphology.
•          Readily distinguished from A. fistularis by the presence of distinctive finger-like or rope-like projections (completely absent in A. fistularis) and by the typically yellowish-brown or brown coloration rather than bright yellow.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The distinctive finger-like or tendril projections are the most diagnostic feature, completely absent in other Aplysina species and instantly identifiable.
•          The yellowish-brown to warm brown exterior contrasts clearly with the bright yellow of A. fistularis and the lavender, pink, or grey tones of A. archeri.
•          The multiple tubes per colony and the smaller tube diameter compared to A. fistularis provide secondary diagnostic features.
•          Unlike encrusting Agelas species, A. insularis is distinctly tubular and erect, with the finger-like projections providing visual texture entirely absent in the smooth-bodied Agelas sponges.
-----

species.name: Callyspongia fallax
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A tubular, branching sponge with erect, cylindrical tubes that rise upward from a shared base. The tubes are characteristically smooth-walled and regularly spaced, often arranged in tight clusters or parallel groupings that give the colony a compact, organized appearance. Color ranges from pale gray-blue to beige, sometimes with slight purple or lavender tints. The overall form is remarkably uniform across colonies, resembling a miniature forest of organ pipes or straws, and individual tubes typically reach 2 to 8 cm in height depending on colony age.
Growth form:
•          Tubes are erect, vertical, and cylindrical, typically ranging from 2 to 8 cm tall depending on colony size and conditions.
•          Individual tubes are relatively uniform in diameter across their length, appearing like straight, rigid pipes without significant tapering.
•          Tubes originate from a common basal platform or spreading base anchored firmly to substrate.
•          Multiple tubes cluster together in a tight, upright fashion, rarely branching laterally or diverging significantly.
•          The overall colony appears highly organized and geometric, in sharp contrast to more irregular branching sponges like Callyspongia vaginalis.
•          Tube tips are blunt and rounded, each terminating in a single visible osculum.
Color:
•          Consistently pale gray, light blue, or beige in most specimens, sometimes with slight purple or lavender tints.
•          Color is uniform along the tube walls and remains consistent across the entire colony without banding.
•          Tips of tubes may appear slightly paler or translucent compared to the tube body.
•          Interior tissue visible through osculum is typically slightly lighter than exterior surface.
•          Color saturation is generally muted and subdued, never vibrant.
Surface features:
•          Tube walls are smooth and even, without pronounced ridges or swellings disrupting the surface.
•          Small, round oscules (exhalant pores) are visible at the tube tips, typically one per tube, appearing as dark, circular openings.
•          The osculum has a slightly raised or everted rim, creating a small crater-like appearance at the tube terminus.
•          Along tube sides, smaller pores are scattered or arranged in loose rows, appearing as pinprick-sized openings.
•          Surface texture is generally smooth and slightly glossy, though biofouling algae or sediment may obscure this.
•          The wall thickness is moderate, neither paper-thin like Niphates digitalis nor heavily inflated like Aplysina fistularis.
Visual context clues:
•          Frequently observed growing on rocky outcrops, coral rubble, or reef walls in areas with moderate current.
•          Colonies often appear isolated or scattered rather than densely packed together.
•          The rigid, upright posture and geometric tube arrangement distinguish it immediately from branching species like Callyspongia vaginalis.
•          Often found alongside stony corals, gorgonians, and other erect reef organisms.
•          In shallow water photos, the regular spacing and parallel arrangement are unmistakable.
•          Small fish and invertebrates may shelter between adjacent tubes, providing additional context cues.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The organized, pipe-like tubes and regular parallel growth instantly separate C. fallax from the more irregular branching of Callyspongia vaginalis.
•          Unlike the thin, spreading tubes of Clathria species, C. fallax tubes are thick, robust, and erect.
•          The single oscule per tube at the tip is diagnostic; most other Callyspongia species have scattered oscules.
•          Distinguished from Desmapsamma anchorata by the smooth tube sides and lack of the distinctive bulbous, lumpy appearance characteristic of Desmapsamma.
-----

species.name: Callyspongia vaginalis
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A striking tubular sponge with tall, slender, trumpet-shaped tubes that rise from the substrate. The tubes are characteristically wide-mouthed at the top, flaring outward like saxophones or flower petals. Colonies typically display pale to bright lime-green coloration in living specimens, with some populations exhibiting cream, tan, or pale gray variants. The overall impression is of an elegant cluster of tall, open-ended vessels arranged vertically and often in partial contact, with dramatic morphological variability between populations from different depths and current regimes.
Growth form:
•          Tubes are tall, erect, and distinctly flared at the upper portion, creating a characteristic trumpet or horn shape.
•          The mouth of each tube is wide and open, often measuring several centimeters in diameter for mature specimens.
•          Tubes originate from a branching base that may divide several times before spreading into multiple erect tubes.
•          Multiple tubes cluster together, sometimes fusing laterally along their sides, creating sheet-like columns of tissue.
•          The overall colony reaches impressive heights, often 15 to 40 cm tall in undisturbed reef environments.
•          Tubes are highly compressible and elastic, visibly collapsing or deforming when current changes.
Color:
•          Living specimens display vibrant lime-green to yellow-green coloration, caused by symbiotic zooxanthellae.
•          Some colonies appear pale cream, tan, or light gray, representing populations without the symbiotic algae.
•          Color is uniform across tube walls and particularly bright along the flared tube rims.
•          Preserved or bleached specimens appear white or pale beige, losing the distinctive green pigmentation.
•          In deeper or low-flow environments, colonies may shift to red or orange tones with darker convoluted ridges.
Surface features:
•          Tube walls are smooth to finely ridged, with subtle texture variations that become evident in close-up photos.
•          The flared tube mouth features a prominent thin rim that may appear slightly darker or more opaque than the tube wall.
•          Oscules are dispersed as small circular openings along the inner surface of the tube mouth and sometimes scattered along lateral tube walls.
•          The interior surface visible within the tube opening may show a subtle radial texture or fine striations.
•          Some morphotypes display deeply convoluted ridges running lengthwise along tubes, creating pronounced textural relief and a wrinkled, accordion-like appearance.
Visual context clues:
•          Commonly found in clear, well-lit reef environments where zooxanthellae thrive, particularly on reef walls, drop-offs, and slope habitats.
•          The bright green coloration is immediately distinctive in shallow water, making identification straightforward in healthy populations.
•          Often observed growing in areas with moderate to strong current, which aids in feeding and gas exchange.
•          Frequently associated with coral-rich environments and rocky outcrops.
•          The flared, open-mouth appearance is unmistakable even from a distance, contrasting sharply with the rigid pipes of C. fallax.
•          Tubes visibly sway and deform in current, a behavioural cue distinct from rigid sponge structures.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The wide-flared tube mouths and trumpet-like shape are instantly diagnostic, separating C. vaginalis from the rigid, straight tubes of C. fallax.
•          The bright green coloration in many populations contrasts sharply with the gray-blue or beige of C. fallax.
•          Unlike Desmapsamma anchorata, which has bulbous, thick-walled tubes, C. vaginalis has thin-walled, elegant tubes with a delicate flared opening.
•          The smooth tube interiors visible at the mouth distinguish it from the encrusting, bumpy surface of Chondrilla caribensis.
-----

species.name: Chondrilla caribensis
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A massive, encrusting to rounded, boulder-like sponge with a thick, heavily convoluted surface covered in prominent bumps, ridges, and lobes. Colonies range from tightly encrusting forms that sprawl across substrate to thick, hemispherical or dome-shaped mounds reaching 50 cm or more in diameter. The surface is characteristically rough and bumpy, resembling a heavily textured brain or crumpled tissue. Color is typically tan, brown, or ochre-yellow, often with darker brown or olive patches and occasional white or light tan ridges, creating a marbled appearance.
Growth form:
•          The sponge grows as an encrusting base that may transition into thick, rounded lobes or massive mounds.
•          The surface is covered with prominent, irregular ridges and valleys that create a brain-like or cerebellar texture.
•          Large conical or rounded bumps project from the surface, often coalescing into ridge systems rather than remaining isolated.
•          The overall form is typically compact and massive, with limited branching or extension.
•          In some environments, the sponge may form thick, plate-like sheets conforming closely to substrate contours.
•          Colony firmly adheres to hard substrate, never freely-standing or stalked.
Color:
•          Predominantly tan, yellowish-brown, or ochre across the main body.
•          Often displays darker brown or olive-colored patches interspersed with lighter areas.
•          White or cream-colored ridges may run along major convoluted features, particularly in deeper or lower-light specimens.
•          Color appears matte or dull rather than glossy, due to the rough surface texture.
•          Some specimens show pale grey-brown tones in heavily shaded habitats.
Surface features:
•          The surface is extensively convoluted with deep ridges, valleys, and sharp creases.
•          Numerous small pores are visible across the surface, appearing as tiny openings interspersed among the ridges.
•          Oscules appear as small, dark circular openings, often tucked within valleys or between ridged features.
•          The texture is rough and granular to the touch, lacking the smooth quality of tube-forming Callyspongia species.
•          Biofouling organisms such as algae and tunicates frequently cover the surface, obscuring underlying texture.
•          Brain-like gyrus patterns of ridges and valleys are diagnostic at close range.
Visual context clues:
•          Found on rocky reefs, cave walls, and sheltered substrate where strong currents are moderate to minimal.
•          Often adjacent to coral colonies and other encrusting sponges, sharing similar habitat preferences.
•          The massive, brain-like appearance is unmistakable and easily identified from moderate distances.
•          Frequently encountered in shadier reef environments compared to the high-light preferences of tube-forming Callyspongia species.
•          The rough, bumpy surface contrasts sharply with the smooth tube walls of Callyspongia species sharing the same reef.
•          Specimens often partially overgrown by algae or coral encrustation, but the underlying ridge pattern remains visible.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The heavy surface convolution and brain-like texture instantly distinguish Chondrilla caribensis from the smooth-walled tubes of both Callyspongia species.
•          Unlike Desmapsamma anchorata, which has distinct tubular lobes, Chondrilla exhibits irregular bumps and ridge systems rather than defined tube-like structures.
•          The encrusting base and massive form differ fundamentally from the erect, trumpet-like growth of C. vaginalis.
•          The tan to brown coloration and dull surface contrast with the bright green often seen in C. vaginalis.
-----

species.name: Desmapsamma anchorata
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A distinctive sponge with erect, thick-walled tubes that rise from a common base, characterized by a bulbous, lumpy appearance unlike the smooth tubes of Callyspongia species. The tubes are notably wider and more robust than those of Callyspongia fallax, with irregular, bumpy surfaces and often conspicuous rounded swellings along their length. Color is typically bright pink to magenta with darker vein-like markings running across the surface, creating a road-map-like pattern that is highly diagnostic. The sponge often grows attached to gorgonian skeletons or coral substrates.
Growth form:
•          Tubes are erect, thick-walled, and distinctly bulbous, with prominent rounded swellings and constrictions along their length.
•          Individual tubes often display an irregular, lumpy profile rather than the smooth cylindrical form of C. fallax.
•          Tubes originate from a spreading, encrusting base, sometimes with pronounced ridges or lobes extending laterally.
•          Multiple tubes cluster together vertically, but the overall arrangement is less geometrically precise than C. fallax.
•          Tubes may reach 10 to 25 cm in height with variable wall thickness, creating a somewhat untidy or organic appearance.
•          The sponge frequently overgrows gorgonian or coral skeletons, using these as internal structural support.
Color:
•          Bright pink to hot pink is the most distinctive feature, sometimes shifting to lavender or pale magenta in shaded specimens.
•          Some specimens display light pink or pale salmon-colored regions, particularly near the oscules.
•          Darker vein-like markings, typically maroon or deep red, create a networked branching pattern across the surface.
•          Color is generally vibrant rather than glossy, and may become obscured by biofouling or sediment.
•          Interior tissue appears darker red or burgundy when visible.
Surface features:
•          Tube walls are distinctly bumpy and irregular, lacking the smooth surface of Callyspongia fallax.
•          The surface texture features numerous small pores scattered across the tube walls in an irregular, non-linear arrangement.
•          Distinctive darker vein-like lines run across the surface in a branching, networked pattern, providing a unique visual signature.
•          Large, dark oscules are visible at tube tips, typically one per tube, with a pronounced, flared or elevated rim.
•          The oscule often appears funnel-shaped or cup-like, creating a distinctive three-dimensional projection.
•          Along tube sides, additional smaller pores and occasional swollen nodules or bumps create an overall lumpy appearance.
Visual context clues:
•          Commonly found on rocky substrate, rubble, and reef walls in moderate to strong current environments.
•          Frequently observed growing alongside other erect sponges and branching corals, often using these as substrate.
•          The bright pink coloration and bulbous tubes are distinctive even at moderate distances underwater.
•          Often encountered in sand patches or rubble zones at mid-depths.
•          The thick, sturdy appearance suggests a robust, current-adapted growth form.
•          May be partially buried under sediment with only pink tips visible above the substrate.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The bumpy, irregular tube surface and bulbous character immediately distinguish D. anchorata from the smooth, uniform tubes of Callyspongia fallax.
•          Unlike Callyspongia vaginalis, which has thin-walled, flared tubes, Desmapsamma tubes are thick-walled and irregular, lacking the elegant trumpet shape.
•          The lumpy, swollen appearance contrasts sharply with the smooth, organized geometry of C. fallax and the delicate spreading form of Clathria.
•          The bright pink color and distinctive vein markings distinguish it from the tan-brown, heavily ridged Chondrilla caribensis.
-----

species.name: Ectyoplasia ferox
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A strikingly massive, rounded to irregular sponge with a thick, solid, bun-like or boulder-like form that dominates reef space. The sponge displays highly variable coloration ranging from brilliant orange-red through golden yellow to tan-brown, often with distinct color zones or patches on a single specimen. The surface is consistently covered with numerous scattered oscules, each surrounded by a slightly raised, often yellow-rimmed rim that creates a characteristic polka-dot or speckled appearance visible across the entire colony surface. Specimens commonly reach 20 to 60 cm in maximum diameter, with the largest exceeding a meter.
Growth form:
•          Massive, roughly spherical to ovoid colonies, typically 20 to 60 cm in maximum diameter.
•          Can reach 1 m or more across in well-established older colonies.
•          Growth form is compact and solid, never branching or tubular.
•          Colonies firmly attached at base, sometimes encrusting basal portions across rock or coral substrate.
•          Surface contours are gently rounded or lumpy, occasionally with shallow lobes or bulges.
•          The sponge may also develop erect chimney-like projections (turret-like structures) rising from the encrusting base.
Color:
•          Bright orange-red to brilliant scarlet in well-lit shallow water, the most common morphotype.
•          Golden yellow to mustard in deeper settings or shaded reef crevices.
•          Tan, brown, or grey-brown in high-sedimentation or silty environments.
•          Color patches or gradients often visible on single specimens, especially older colonies.
•          Yellow-rimmed oscules contrast sharply against darker body color, creating the distinctive speckled appearance.
•          Interior tissue is distinctly yellow, providing strong contrast with the brown or orange exterior.
Surface features:
•          Numerous round to oval oscules scattered across the entire surface, typically 30 to 100 or more per large specimen.
•          Each oscule is typically 3 to 8 mm diameter, with a distinctly raised, rim-like collar (often yellow, orange, or cream colored).
•          Surface between oscules is smooth to slightly granular, sometimes with fine bumps or warts.
•          Oscules are evenly distributed across the body rather than clustered.
•          No pronounced ridges, spines, or branching structures disrupt the surface.
•          The texture has a felt-like or velvety quality in close-up.
Visual context clues:
•          One of the most conspicuous reef sponges, highly visible from distance due to massive size and bold coloration.
•          Often partially tucked beneath reef ledges or in shaded crevices, with the bright color contrasting against shadowed substrate.
•          Specimens are typically solitary or loosely scattered, not gregarious or clustered.
•          Often positioned in moderate to high water flow zones where feeding current is strong.
•          The yellow oscule collars are visible from a distance and serve as a key field identification cue.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Massive rounded form combined with scattered prominent yellow-rimmed oscules is absolutely diagnostic.
•          Color intensity is immediately distinctive; no other large Caribbean sponge displays such saturated orange-red.
•          Polka-dot appearance (oscule pattern) is unique among massive Caribbean sponges.
•          Distinguished from Scopalina ruetzleri by larger size, heavier build, and yellow oscule collars rather than orange overall coloration.
•          Distinguished from Monanchora arbuscula by brown or orange coloration with yellow collars rather than red with white collars.
-----

species.name: Halisarca caerulea
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
An exceptionally thin, delicate, gel-like encrusting sponge ranging from sky blue to violet in color, with an extremely distinctive regularly spaced star-shaped network of superficial canals radiating outward from central oscules. The sponge is so thin and translucent at edges that it appears almost membranous, giving it an almost ephemeral quality despite its leathery consistency. Patches typically cover dead coral skeleton or rock in cryptic reef habitats, where the bright blue color contrasts dramatically against shaded substrates.
Growth form:
•          Paper-thin encrusting sheets, typically 1 to 2 mm thick, occasionally 3 to 4 mm in deeper settings.
•          Patches range from a few square centimetres to over 50 cm² across.
•          Forms low, flat, continuous coverage over dead coral skeleton or rock.
•          Leathery consistency despite extreme thinness.
•          Edges often thin to translucent; may appear slightly lifted from substrate.
•          No tubes, lobes, or branching structures ever present.
Color:
•          Sky blue to bright blue in most populations.
•          Violet to pale purple in shaded habitats or deeper settings.
•          Color remarkably uniform across the surface, without patches or banding.
•          More vibrant and saturated blue than any other Caribbean sponge.
•          Interior tissue (visible if scratched) is slightly paler blue.
Surface features:
•          Absolutely smooth and shiny surface except for the canal pattern; completely free of texture, bumps, or spines.
•          Distinctive star-shaped networks of shallow canals radiating outward from each osculum.
•          Each star is typically 1 to 3 cm across, with canals becoming progressively shallower toward the star’s edges.
•          Stars are regularly spaced, typically 1 to 3 cm apart, arranged in a near-uniform grid.
•          Oscules are small (2 to 3 mm diameter) and centrally located in each star.
•          The geometric regularity of the canal pattern is a key visual signature.
Visual context clues:
•          Found in cryptic reef microhabitats, especially under coral overhangs, in cavities, and at cave entrances.
•          Often completely shaded or partially covered by sediment or macroalgae, with the bright blue color emerging suddenly when light strikes it.
•          The paper-thin profile means the sponge is often easily overlooked despite its bright color.
•          Frequently growing alongside other cryptic encrusting fauna (small ascidians, encrusting algae) in dim microhabitats.
•          The star-shaped canal pattern is visible even from moderate distances when lit obliquely.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Blue color combined with star-shaped canal patterns is instantly diagnostic; no other Caribbean sponge shares this combination.
•          Geometric regularity of star pattern is immediately recognisable even in low-resolution photos.
•          Extreme thinness and smooth, glossy surface contrast sharply with all encrusting sponges of similar colour.
•          Uniform spacing of stars suggests almost artificial precision, distinguishing it from any naturally textured surface.
•          Differs from blue-tinted Niphates digitalis by being encrusting rather than tubular.
-----

species.name: Iotrochota birotulata
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A delicate, profusely branching sponge with an intricate skeletal form composed of thin, ribbon-like or rope-like branches that spread irregularly in multiple directions. The sponge is characterised by yellowish-green to pale yellow-tan body color, with distinctly darker brown or black edges on branches that create a striking two-tone outlined appearance. The overall colony resembles a lacy three-dimensional net or skeletal framework rather than a solid mass, and individual specimens reach 10 to 40 cm in height, occasionally larger.
Growth form:
•          Extensively branching colonies with thin cylindrical to flattened branches, typically 3 to 5 mm in diameter.
•          Branches spread in multiple directions, often at acute angles, creating complex three-dimensional structures.
•          Anastomosing (interconnecting) branches form irregular meshes or networks.
•          Colonies typically 10 to 40 cm tall, occasionally reaching 50 cm or more in protected settings.
•          Branch edges often wavy or undulating rather than perfectly straight.
•          No obvious central trunk; branching pattern appears almost random and organic.
Color:
•          Yellowish-green to pale yellow as the dominant body color.
•          Dark brown to black edges on branch tips and branch margins are distinctive.
•          Color contrast between branch centers and dark edges creates a striped or outlined appearance.
•          Color is consistent across branches, but the edge-darkening remains the diagnostic feature.
•          Interior tissue slightly darker than surface, visible when branches are damaged.
Surface features:
•          Smooth, slightly glossy surface on branches.
•          Wavy or scalloped branch margins visible on close inspection.
•          Fine oscules scattered irregularly along branch surfaces and edges.
•          Branch surface sometimes shows subtle ridging or fluting running lengthwise.
•          No pronounced spines, tubercles, or conical projections.
•          Branch tips often appear slightly tapered or bluntly rounded.
Visual context clues:
•          Highly distinctive lacy, mesh-like silhouette visible even from distance.
