•          Found in moderate to high-flow reef environments, exposed reef faces, and coral rubble zones.
•          Often positioned perpendicular to water flow, catching current with its branched form.
•          Branches frequently intertwined with coral or gorgonian skeletons, using them as structural support.
•          Often photographed with small fish or invertebrates sheltering in the open spaces between branches.
•          The two-tone outlined branches create a distinctive visual signature recognizable from several meters away.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Thin branching form combined with dark-edged branches and yellowish-green color are uniquely characteristic.
•          Mesh-like, intricate branching pattern immediately distinguishes from massive or encrusting sponges.
•          Two-tone coloration (pale centers with dark edges) is diagnostic among branching sponges.
•          Contrast with other branching sponges: Iotrochota birotulata is much more delicate and intricate than Ircinia species.
•          Differs from Aplysina species by being greenish rather than yellow or purple, and by having darker branch margins.
-----

species.name: Ircinia felix
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A highly morphologically variable sponge occurring as either massive, compact, rounded or bulbous forms or sprawling, flat, plate-like sheets. The sponge is characterised by dense surface pore coverage, dark oscules scattered across the surface, and variable coloration ranging from dark greenish-brown through tan to whitish, often with visible color patterning or blotching. The surface displays a consistently granular to bumpy texture from small pore projections, and the conulose surface pattern is one of its most reliable visual cues.
Growth form (Massive morphotype):
•          Thick, compact, roughly spherical to irregular ovoid colonies, typically 20 to 50 cm across.
•          Solid, boulder-like form with rounded or bulging lobes.
•          Base firmly attached to substrate without distinct stalks.
•          Surface contours gently undulating with shallow, rounded lobes rather than pointed projections.
•          Colony presents a single, integrated mass rather than multiple discrete lobes.
Growth form (Sprawling morphotype):
•          Flat, plate-like to sheet-like growth form, sometimes with irregular shallow lobes or ruffled edges.
•          Thickness typically 1 to 4 cm, occasionally reaching 5 to 8 cm in older specimens.
•          Spreads across rock, coral rubble, or dead coral skeletal areas.
•          Often partially overlapping other colonies or substrate features.
•          The sprawling form may cover several square meters of substrate in extensive colonies.
Color:
•          Brown, red-brown, or gray externally in massive morphotype.
•          Whitish to pale tan or pale grey-brown in sprawling morphotype.
•          Tan to light brown internally, distinctly lighter than the exterior, providing strong visual contrast.
•          Two-tone appearance is striking, with darker exterior and warmer paler interior visible at any breaks or oscules.
•          Dark oscules create strong contrast against the body color.
Surface features:
•          Densely conulose: surface covered with tiny bumps 0.5 to 2 mm high, spaced 3 to 5 mm apart.
•          Conules are consistent and uniform, creating a finely textured, pebbly appearance rather than irregular bumps.
•          Lattice-like pattern sometimes evident where conules merge or align.
•          Oscules are small, 3 to 6 mm, flush or slightly elevated, not rimmed with contrasting collars.
•          Triangular incurrent sieves may be visible as fine meshwork on the sponge face.
•          Surface texture is highly diagnostic at close range due to the regular pebbly pattern.
Visual context clues:
•          Found on exposed reef faces, slopes, and hard substrate, often on well-lit surfaces with moderate current.
•          Commonly encrusts coral rubble, rock, and dead coral.
•          May be covered with sediment or overgrown by algae in older colonies, but the bumpy texture remains visible through coverings.
•          Both morphotypes may occur sympatrically on the same reef, requiring careful examination of surface features.
•          Often photographed alongside other massive sponges and encrusting fauna, where its dense pebbly surface is uniquely recognizable.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Brown or grey body combined with dense fine uniform conular texture (pebbly) and small oscules without contrasting collars is collectively diagnostic.
•          Distinguished from Scopalina ruetzleri (orange, larger lumpy bumps), Ectyoplasia ferox (chimneys, yellow collars), and Monanchora arbuscula (red, white collars).
•          The consistent pebbly surface combined with brown exterior and tan interior at damaged edges are the strongest cues.
•          Differs from Ircinia strobilina (which is darker, more uniformly spherical, and has larger oscular depressions).
-----

species.name: Ircinia strobilina
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A dense, globular, or slightly lobate massive sponge with a distinctive dark gray to black exterior forming a characteristically rounded ball or dome shape that typically measures 0.3 to 0.6 m (1 to 2 ft) across. The surface is uniformly bumpy with numerous small conical projections distributed evenly across the entire form. Large excurrent pores create prominent dark depressions visible at the top and upper sides, while many small incurrent pores are scattered across the lower surface.
Growth form:
•          The overall structure is massive and globular, growing as a single integrated unit without branching or extending lobes.
•          The sponge maintains a roughly spherical profile, sometimes with minor bulges or slight lobation that does not disrupt the overall dome shape.
•          Growth is sedentary and firmly anchored to the substrate, with no peduncle or stalk extending from the base.
•          The surface topography is dominated by conules that are closely packed and interconnected by fine ridges rather than forming an orderly lattice.
•          The body is solid and dense throughout, with no obvious hollow chambers visible from outside.
Color:
•          The exterior is consistently dark gray to black, appearing very uniform and showing minimal variation across the surface.
•          The interior is tan to light brown, visible at any breaks or damage, creating a strong contrast with the dark exterior.
•          Some specimens display darker charcoal-gray tones with subtle mottled patches that do not obscure the overall dark appearance.
•          The color appears deepest at the apex and may lighten marginally on side surfaces.
•          No white, red, or purple tones are present on healthy specimens.
Surface features:
•          Densely distributed conules cover the entire surface, creating a distinctly spiny or bumpy tactile texture.
•          Conules are fine and closely spaced, rather than widely separated or prominent, giving a granular appearance.
•          Large excurrent pores form dark, funnel-like depressions that are easily visible with the naked eye.
•          Small incurrent pores are uniformly distributed and more numerous on the lower and side surfaces than on the apex.
•          The surface lacks visible oscula-like apertures as distinct openings, instead appearing as part of the conule pattern.
•          The overall texture is smooth relative to the spine height rather than rough and ragged.
Visual context clues:
•          The sponge appears as a distinctive basketball- or golf-ball-like object sitting firmly on the reef floor.
•          Dark silhouettes stand out dramatically against lighter sandy substrates and pale coral skeletons.
•          Specimens are typically solitary or in small, well-spaced groups rather than clustering densely.
•          The entire upper hemisphere is usually exposed to light and water flow, rarely buried.
•          When viewed from above, the apex oscules appear as darker spots creating a characteristic focal point.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The combination of dark gray-black color, spherical shape, and spiny surface is immediately unmistakable and requires no magnification to identify.
•          Mycale laxissima differs by displaying bright red-orange coloration, branching lobes, and a much smaller overall size (5-15 cm vs 30-60 cm).
•          Neofibularia nolitangere differs by being much larger (up to 1 m), having visible large irregular oscula, and displaying brown rather than black coloration.
•          Iotrochota birotulata differs by forming thin rope-like branches rather than a compact sphere and by displaying greenish coloration.
-----

species.name: Monanchora arbuscula
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A vivid scarlet to deep crimson encrusting sponge forming cushioned, lumpy mounds or low bushy masses on shallow reef substrates. The most striking feature is a constellation of small oscula distributed evenly across the surface, each surrounded by a conspicuous white or pale collar membrane that radiates outward like a star or halo, creating a immediately distinctive speckled, multi-punctate appearance that is visible even from several meters away. The sponge typically forms compact masses 2 to 4 cm thick and spreads 15 to 30 cm across the substrate.
Growth form:
•          The growth form is encrusting to sub-massive, typically 1 to 3 cm thick and spreading laterally across the substrate.
•          The sponge forms soft, cushioned mounds with gently rounded lobes rather than a flat sheet.
•          A thin, semi-transparent whitish membrane often covers the surface, giving the tissue a slightly veiled or opalescent appearance.
•          Oscula are small (0.3 to 2 cm in diameter) and regularly scattered across the surface at relatively uniform spacing.
•          Each osculum is surrounded by a distinctive white or pale collar that stands out sharply against the red body tissue.
Color:
•          The external surface is brilliant scarlet, crimson, or deep red without orange or purple tones.
•          The color is saturated and vibrant, remaining easily visible even in deeper water or dim lighting.
•          The interior is darker red or burgundy when visible through tissue or at breaks.
•          White collar membranes around each osculum provide a stark contrast against the red body.
•          Some specimens may display slightly deeper red patches but overall coloration remains uniformly bright red.
Surface features:
•          The surface is soft, smooth, and slightly granular rather than conulose or heavily textured.
•          White-rimmed oscula are the dominant surface feature, each surrounded by a raised or distinct collar of pale tissue.
•          The osculum rims are pale cream to white, creating a bold color contrast with the red body.
•          The tissue is compressible and yields to gentle pressure, indicating a soft body structure.
•          No prominent ridges, tubes, or grooves disrupt the gently undulating surface topography.
Visual context clues:
•          The sponge appears as a brilliant red patch with a white-speckled or starry surface pattern when viewed from above.
•          Found on shallow reef surfaces, coral rubble, and hard substrates exposed to moderate light (typically 2 to 10 m depth).
•          Often growing directly on exposed coral heads or smooth hard reef substrate.
•          The bright red color stands out distinctly against darker reef surfaces, pale coral skeleton, and sand.
•          May be partially overgrown by zoanthids or algae on edges, but the central red area with white oscula remains clearly visible.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The vivid red coloration combined with white-rimmed oscula arranged in a speckled pattern is immediately diagnostic and unmistakable.
•          The white oscula collars are the single most distinguishing feature, present on no other common Caribbean encrusting sponge.
•          Scopalina ruetzleri differs by displaying orange (not scarlet red) coloration, lacking white-collared oscula, and showing a distinctly conulose surface.
•          Ectyoplasia ferox differs by being brown (not red), having yellow-collared oscula (not white), and forming tall, erect chimney structures.
-----

species.name: Mycale laxissima
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A delicate, ramose-lobate sponge displaying vivid bright red to deep red-orange coloration that creates a striking visual appearance on the reef. The sponge forms multiple upright or semi-erect lobes and branches rising from a common base, creating a dense, clustered appearance reminiscent of a bunch of strawberries or grouped vase forms. Individual lobes or branches are 2 to 5 cm wide and 5 to 15 cm tall, with the entire sponge typically reaching 12 to 25 cm in overall height. The surface displays a characteristically rough, granular texture, and the interior is lighter pinkish-red or tan when visible.
Growth form:
•          The structure is ramose-lobate, with multiple finger-like or bushy lobes radiating upward from a compact common base.
•          Individual lobes are rounded at tips and partially separated at their base, creating a clustered bouquet-like arrangement.
•          The sponge is semi-rigid to somewhat flexible, allowing slight movement and bending in moderate to strong currents.
•          No single dominant trunk or primary axis exists; instead, growth is multidirectional and symmetrical.
•          Height typically exceeds width, giving the sponge an upright, columnar overall profile.
Color:
•          The external surface is bright red to deep red-orange, representing one of the most saturated red tones visible on Caribbean reefs.
•          Some specimens display deep crimson to scarlet without orange tones, while others show peachy-orange accents.
•          The color is consistent across all lobes without patterning, banding, or spots.
•          The interior is tan, cream, or pale pinkish-red when visible through breaks or at the base.
•          Color remains vivid even in dim light, and no bleaching or discoloration patterns are typical.
Surface features:
•          The surface displays a granular or bumpy texture composed of densely packed small incurrent pores.
•          Fine pore rows are visible with magnification, running in linear patterns along the length of lobes.
•          The surface resembles fine sandpaper rather than being smooth or glossy.
•          Small oscules are inconspicuous among the pore pattern and do not form prominent openings.
•          The texture is tactilely coarse when touched, lacking the soft, smooth quality of some encrusting sponges.
Visual context clues:
•          The sponge stands out as one of the brightest red-orange objects on the reef, visible from several meters away.
•          Found on sandy areas, seagrass beds, rubble zones, and transitional reef environments rather than on coral heads.
•          Often partially buried or emerging from sand with lobes extending upward from a base at or below the substrate surface.
•          The upright lobes create a distinctive vertical profile when viewed in situ, contrasting with surrounding branching corals or gorgonians.
•          Specimens frequently display fine sediment particles clinging to the granular surface.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The vivid red-orange coloration combined with delicate, finger-like lobes is diagnostic.
•          Iotrochota birotulata differs by displaying blackish-green coloration, thicker rope-like branches, and a scrambling, tangled growth form.
•          Ircinia strobilina differs by being dark gray-black, massive and globular, and lacking lobes or branches entirely.
•          Neofibularia nolitangere differs by being much larger (30 cm to 1 m), displaying brown rather than orange coloration, and forming lumpy irregular masses with large prominent oscula.
-----

species.name: Neofibularia nolitangere
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A large, irregular massive sponge with a prominent lumpy, lobate form displaying deep brown to dark reddish-brown coloration across much of the visible surface. The sponge grows as a compact, rounded mass that typically measures 30 cm tall and 30 cm wide, though large specimens reach 1 m or more in width. The topography is characteristically uneven and bumpy with multiple large rounded lobes and irregular bulging projections distributed unevenly. Large oscula are visible as dark, prominent depressions concentrated at the apex and upper sides, creating a distinctive pitted appearance.
Growth form:
•          The structure is massive and strongly lobate, with multiple rounded lobes of varying sizes projecting from a central mass.
•          The sponge is thick and solid with internal cavities that support the large oscula visible from outside.
•          Growth is sedentary and firmly anchored to the substrate without any peduncle or stalk.
•          The overall outline is highly irregular and asymmetrical, with bulges occurring at different positions on different specimens.
•          Lobes are rounded and blunt rather than pointed or tapering, giving the form a bulbous, lumpy appearance.
Color:
•          The exterior is deep brown to dark reddish-brown, displaying a uniform coloration without patterning or banding.
•          Some specimens show maroon or burgundy tinges, particularly on lower and shaded lobes.
•          The interior is tan to light tan, visible at breaks, providing a striking contrast with the dark exterior.
•          The color appears nearly black in dim light or deep water, but always retains a brown rather than gray tone.
•          No other colors (red, orange, yellow, white) appear on healthy specimens.
Surface features:
•          The surface is rough and bumpy with numerous irregular protrusions and depressions.
•          Large, conspicuous oscula form dark funnel-like or crater-like depressions that are easily visible without magnification.
•          Small incurrent pores are scattered across the surface but are much less conspicuous than the large oscula.
•          The surface appears somewhat granular or pitted with a tactilely coarse texture.
•          Smooth outer surface areas alternate with rougher interior cavity surfaces visible at breaks.
Visual context clues:
•          The sponge appears distinctly large and heavy-looking compared to most other reef sponges.
•          Brown-red coloration creates strong contrast against sandy substrates, pale coral skeletons, and lighter rubble.
•          Specimens typically appear solitary, maintaining distance from other individuals, rather than clustering.
•          The entire form is usually exposed and accessible on the reef, rarely buried or overgrown.
•          The multiple lumpy lobes create an unmistakably irregular silhouette when viewed in profile.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The combination of large size (30 cm to 1 m), deep brown coloration, irregular lumpy lobes, and visible large oscula is uniquely diagnostic.
•          Iotrochota birotulata differs by forming thin, rope-like branches rather than a massive lumpy form and by displaying greenish coloration.
•          Ircinia strobilina differs by being smaller (30 to 60 cm), uniformly spherical, and dark gray-black rather than brown.
•          Mycale laxissima differs by being much smaller (12 to 25 cm), bright red-orange, and formed of delicate branching lobes.
-----

species.name: Neopetrosia proxima
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A highly variable sponge ranging from thin encrusting sheets to massive lobed or branching formations, characterised by purplish-brown, maroon, or dark brown coloration that varies substantially between geographic populations. The sponge typically forms thick spreading masses on substrate (coral rubble, sand, or rock), with regular to irregularly shaped lobes that are typically 3 to 5 cm tall and 5 to 15 cm across, creating a lumpy, cushioned topography. The exterior is brown, purplish-brown, or maroon, while the interior is light tan, visible at breaks or margins.
Growth form:
•          The form is encrusting to massive and spreads laterally across substrate in preference to growing upright.
•          Lobes are rounded and cushioned with gently curved surfaces rather than sharp edges or pointed projections.
•          Occasional finger-like projections occur in some populations, creating a weakly branching appearance.
•          The sponge covers considerable substrate area while maintaining relatively uniform thickness throughout.
•          Margins between lobes are rounded and blunt, and edges are not convoluted or highly irregular.
Color:
•          The exterior is brown, purplish-brown, or maroon, with significant color variation between geographic populations.
•          Some specimens are predominantly pink or purple, while others are yellowish-tan or brownish-tan.
•          The color is uniform across the surface without patterning, spots, or banding.
•          The interior is light tan, creating a pale contrast with the darker exterior.
•          The surface has a matte finish without iridescence or gloss.
Surface features:
•          The surface is smooth to slightly uneven, lacking the rough, bumpy texture of Neofibularia.
•          Small incurrent pores are scattered across the surface but are not prominent or densely packed.
•          Larger oscula are visible as slightly raised or slightly depressed openings but are not the dominant surface feature.
•          The surface is considerably less textured than Neofibularia but more uneven than some glossy encrusting sponges.
•          The edges of lobes are smooth and rounded rather than sharp or folded.
Visual context clues:
•          The sponge appears as thick, spreading cushions on reef rubble and sandy areas.
•          Specimens are typically partially covered by sand or fine rubble, with exposed portions showing color clearly.
•          Found in well-lit shallow to moderate reef environments where other massive sponges are less common.
•          Solitary masses or sparse scattered groups are typical, with individuals maintaining separation.
•          The lumpy lobe pattern creates distinctive hills and valleys when viewed from above.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          The spreading lobed form with purplish-brown to maroon coloration and light tan interior are the primary diagnostic features.
•          Iotrochota birotulata differs by forming thin rope-like branches that weave and intertwine and by displaying greenish coloration.
•          Ircinia strobilina differs by being spherical, dark gray-black, and much smaller without lobes.
•          Mycale laxissima differs by being bright red-orange, forming delicate upright lobes, and much smaller overall.
-----
-----

species.name: Niphates digitalis
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A distinctive vase or cup-shaped sponge with thin, delicate walls that range from blue-gray to lavender, occasionally showing pale pink tones. The structure consists of a narrow stalk (peduncle) that flares open into a broad, cup-like aperture at the top, creating an elegant tubular form. The entire sponge is tissue-thin and translucent, particularly at the rim where light passes through the wall structure, and it typically grows to 30 to 50 cm in height. The overall silhouette is one of graceful verticality, standing prominently upright on the reef.
Growth form:
•          Tubular or vase-shaped primary structure with a distinct peduncle and open cup aperture.
•          Narrow stalk transitions progressively to a broad, open rim without branching.
•          Solitary growth: individual sponges do not cluster; each stands alone on the substrate.
•          Occasionally displays fan-like variants in some populations, with widened top margins.
•          Typical height ranges from 30 to 50 cm in mature specimens, though larger individuals occur in deeper water.
•          Wall thickness is uniformly thin along the entire structure.
Color:
•          Blue-gray to lavender is the dominant coloration, despite the misleading common name.
•          Pale pink or purplish tones appear in some individuals, particularly at the base or peduncle.
•          Translucent rim at the cup opening allows light to illuminate internal tissue, revealing pale cream or yellowish interior.
•          Color remains relatively uniform throughout the wall tissue without banding or patches.
•          Darker at the base and progressively lighter toward the rim in most specimens.
Surface features:
•          Thin, fragile wall texture with visible pores scattered across the external surface.
•          Lacy, frayed margins characteristic of the cup opening, often appearing delicately torn or threadlike at the rim.
•          Delicate, tissue-thin construction visible in the translucent areas, especially near the top edge.
•          Scattered oscules distributed along the upper edge and lateral walls, appearing as small openings.
•          Smooth overall surface between perforations, lacking bumps, ridges, or conules; the texture is uniformly smooth and slightly glossy.
•          The vase interior surface may be slightly textured with shallow ridges.
Visual context clues:
•          Stands prominently and vertically on reef substrate, easily visible from a distance due to upright form.
•          The vase profile creates a distinctive silhouette especially when backlit against open water.
•          Partially colonized by algae or zoanthids on the outer wall surface in some specimens, creating a patchy appearance.
•          Silhouetted strongly against reef background when backlit, making the vase profile unmistakable in profile views.
•          Lacks the thick, robust appearance of larger Caribbean tube sponges, appearing delicate by comparison.
•          Often photographed with small fish hovering inside the cup, attracted to the protected space.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Distinctive vase profile is the most reliable field identification feature, recognizable in profile views from meters away.
•          Thin, translucent walls allow light to visibly pass through the rim, a feature absent in thick-walled tube sponges.
•          Open cup aperture at the apex is the defining structural character, never branched or closed.
•          Lack of spines, bumps, or conulose texture distinguishes from most encrusting and massive sponges.
•          Blue-gray to lavender coloration distinctly separates it from warm-colored (Callyspongia pink, Aiolochroia white) tube sponges.
•          Distinguished from Niphates erecta (branched, multiple fingers, gray-purple with zoanthids) by the single unbranched cup structure.
-----

species.name: Niphates erecta
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A branched, rope-like or finger-like sponge structurally distinct from the vase-shaped N. digitalis. The structure consists of multiple erect cylindrical branches that grow vertically or at angles, often creating a tangled or interwoven appearance. The branches are typically porous and textured rather than smooth, with an overall stockier, more robust feel than the delicate vase sponge. Growth habit often forms dense masses or tangled strands that frequently appear heavily colonized by zoanthids, which can completely obscure the underlying lavender sponge color with a brownish or multicolored crust.
Growth form:
•          Multiple erect, cylindrical branches or finger-like projections sprouting from a common base.
•          Repent and erect branching pattern with some horizontal runners at the base and vertical columns rising upward.
•          Stalk-like or column-shaped individual branches, each typically 1 to 3 cm in diameter.
•          Can reach 90 cm or more in total height, often the dominant structure in deep reef cryptic habitats.
•          Often tangled or interwoven with neighbouring branches, creating dense aggregations rather than isolated individuals.
•          Branch tips are rounded or blunt, occasionally showing slight tapering.
Color:
•          Lavender to pale purple primary coloration of the exposed sponge tissue.
•          Grayish-white bases and middle sections visible where the sponge is not colonized.
•          Pinkish tones distributed throughout the exposed tissue in some specimens.
•          Often appears heavily encrusted or brownish due to dense zoanthid colonisation, which can completely mask the underlying sponge color.
•          Zoanthid coverage variable: some specimens show vibrant sponge color, while others are nearly entirely obscured by symbiotic organisms.
Surface features:
•          Porous, bumpy texture with visible pores densely scattered across the branch surfaces.
•          Frilly or convoluted surface that is distinctly less smooth than the vase sponge, with a wrinkled or rippled appearance.
•          Scattered oscules distributed along the length of each branch rather than concentrated at the apex.
•          Densely covered with commensal organisms including zoanthids and hydroids that create a “furry” or “hairy” appearance.
•          Zoanthid polyps often create small knob-like clusters across the surface, obscuring the underlying sponge texture.
•          Branch surface visible between zoanthids reveals fine pore distribution.
Visual context clues:
•          Often the dominant structure in cryptic reef habitats, found heavily branched or sprawling.
•          Creates thick tangles and extensive aggregations on the reef, often filling protected overhangs and caves.
•          Zoanthid companions are nearly universal and diagnostic: a sponge without zoanthid colonization is unlikely to be N. erecta.
•          Multiple branches sprouting upward readily distinguish it from the single-stemmed, unbranched vase profile of N. digitalis.
•          Visible interconnection between branches at the base indicates strong growth integration unlike isolated tube sponges.
•          Often photographed with small fish sheltering between the dense branches.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Multiple erect branches or fingers sprouting upward from a common base, never a single unified cup structure.
•          Lavender to gray coloration, often heavily covered or obscured by multicolored zoanthid colonies.
•          Convoluted, textured surface with visible pores and wrinkles, distinctly rougher than smooth tube sponge walls.
•          Small, colorful clustered zoanthid polyps visible across the surface as a diagnostic feature.
•          Stockier, more robust overall appearance compared to the delicate, thin-walled vase sponge N. digitalis.
•          Readily distinguished from Niphates digitalis (single vase, smooth, thin-walled) by the presence of multiple branches and zoanthid colonization.
-----

species.name: Oceanapia bartschi
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A distinctive ball-and-stalk structure with a characteristic spherical or bulbous main body buried in sediment or rubble, connected via a long, thin vertical chimney that rises prominently to the reef surface. The overall morphology is uniquely two-chambered: the majority of the sponge body remains cryptic and hidden underground, while only the upright tube portion extends visibly above into the water column. The visible tube is relatively narrow and unbranched, creating a striking vertical silhouette, and the entire structure is typically 30 to 50 cm or taller. The surface of the chimney displays characteristic erect fistule projections that give it a distinctive bumpy or stubbly appearance.
Growth form:
•          Subterranean bulb buried in sand, rubble, or sediment, the true body of the sponge.
•          Long, thin upright chimney is the exhalant tube visible above substrate.
•          Chimney is solitary, unbranched, and relatively smooth-walled between fistule projections.
•          Chimneys typically reach 30 to 50 cm or greater in height above the substrate.
•          Highly collared oscule at the apex with a thick, distinctly raised rim that appears as a pronounced collar.
•          Individual sponges are solitary and do not cluster, each occupying discrete sediment area.
Color:
•          Tan, beige, or pale yellowish overall, the most consistent diagnostic color feature.
•          Cream-colored tube walls visible in most specimens, occasionally with slight iridescence.
•          Occasional reddish or brownish tones where sediment grains adhere to the sticky sponge surface.
•          Base and chimney transition often slightly darker than the upper portions, particularly where sediment is incorporated.
•          Colors remain relatively muted and monochromatic, without banding, patches, or dramatic color shifts.
Surface features:
•          Erect fistules (small inhalant tubes) densely scattered across the chimney wall, covering most of the external surface.
•          Transparent or translucent rim at the oscule opening, allowing observation of water flow at the apex.
•          Highly collared oscule with a thick, distinctly raised rim that often appears as a pronounced lip or flange.
•          Fistules appear as small, pore-like projections ranging from 1 to 2 mm in height, creating a “bumpy” or “stubbly” texture.
•          Relatively smooth wall between fistule projections, lacking the heavy conulation seen in other encrusting sponges.
Visual context clues:
•          Solitary stalk rising vertically from substrate is immediately diagnostic in field conditions.
•          The buried portion is rarely visible unless the sponge is dislodged by storm or disturbance.
•          May be surrounded by a clear or scoured zone of sediment influenced by strong exhalant flow from the oscule.
•          Stands prominently upright without crowding or clustering, unlike many small encrusting sponges.
•          The vertical chimney silhouette against sandy bottom is unmistakable from any reasonable angle.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Single upright chimney protruding from buried bulb, the most reliable field character.
•          Pale tan or cream coloration that stands out against darker reef substrate or sediment.
•          Erect fistules covering the entire chimney surface, creating a distinctive bumpy or warty appearance.
•          Raised, collared oscule rim at the apex; the oscule is never flush or inconspicuous.
•          Solitary, unbranched tube structure that never bifurcates, distinguishing it from branched sponges like Niphates erecta.
•          Distinguished from other unbranched tube sponges by the dense fistule covering (versus scattered oscules) and pale coloration.
-----

species.name: Plakortis angulospiculatus
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A low-profile encrusting sponge that forms soft, rounded cushions or gentle lobes on hard substrate without projecting vertically or branching. The entire structure remains compact and mound-like, typically only a few centimeters in height despite spreading laterally across the rock. The surface is characteristically smooth or only slightly convoluted, lacking the bumpy, spiky, or ridged textures found on other encrusting species. The sponge has a waxy or soapy appearance that is immediately apparent: the tissue appears slick and slightly shiny rather than matte or velvety, a feature reflecting its viscous chemical nature.
Growth form:
•          Encrusting cushions or soft lobes as the primary growth habit.
•          Low-profile, rarely exceeding a few centimeters in vertical relief from substrate.
•          Forms rounded mounds or gently domed cushions on hard rock or dead coral substrate.
•          Broad lateral spread from a single basal attachment area.
•          Non-branching, non-tubular form, never producing upright projections or distinct tubes.
•          Colonies typically spread 7 to 20 cm across while remaining low.
Color:
•          Dark brown to very dark green primary coloration, the most consistent and diagnostic color.
•          Gray to grayish-white accents visible in some individuals, particularly in areas of tissue thinning.
•          Light brown variants occur occasionally within the same species, showing phenotypic color variation.
•          Generally muted, earthy tones without bright pigments or iridescence.
•          Color remains consistent throughout the tissue without banding, patches, or internal color differentiation.
Surface features:
•          Smooth to slightly convoluted surface texture, much smoother than most other encrusting sponges.
•          Crater-like or cup-shaped oscules scattered across the surface, appearing as small depressions or openings.
•          Waxy or soapy texture: slick to the touch, reflecting the viscous nature of the tissue; the surface appears slightly shiny rather than matte.
•          Scattered small pores across the surface between oscules, visible only under close inspection.
•          Minimal protrusions: the surface remains mostly flat or gently rounded, lacking bumps or ridges.
Visual context clues:
•          The dark, low cushion form often blends with shadowed reef substrates, making the sponge easy to overlook.
•          Often partially cryptic, occurring in crevices, overhangs, or on shaded reef walls.
•          Dark coloration aids recognition in dim light or cryptic habitats where bright sponges would stand out.
•          Gelatinous appearance makes it look distinctly different from crusty or granular encrusting forms.
•          The slick, almost wet-looking surface is visible as a subtle sheen in good lighting, distinguishing it from matte sponges.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Smooth, cushion-like mound with no vertical projections or tubular structures.
•          Dark brown or very dark green color immediately recognizable in most lighting conditions.
•          Small crater-like oscules scattered across the surface, appearing as small dark openings.
•          Encrusting form that stays low and broad across the substrate, never forming upright projections.
•          Waxy or slick appearance distinguishes it from bumpy (Monanchora), grainy (Spirastrella), or ridged (Raspaciona) encrusting forms.
•          Distinguished from Mycale laxissima (bright red-orange, finely branching) and Neofibularia nolitangere (massive, conulose, prominent oscula) by dark color and smooth form.
-----

species.name: Scopalina ruetzleri
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A small, bright orange encrusting sponge with an instantly recognizable lumpy, bumpy, or warty surface texture caused by densely packed conical projections. The sponge typically forms plump, cushioned mounds that grow upward rather than spreading as flat sheets, creating a three-dimensional, knobbly appearance. The coloration is uniformly vivid orange throughout, remaining unmistakable even in low light conditions, and the tissue has a soft, gelatinous quality that is easily compressible and fragile. Individual specimens rarely exceed 2 cm in vertical relief and are typically smaller than most other encrusting sponges, making them appear as small bright lumps on the reef.
Growth form:
•          Encrusting habit with thin to thick vertical relief, from 0.5 cm to 2 cm in height above substrate.
•          Plump, cushioned profile that grows upward in a lumpy mass rather than spreading as a flat sheet.
•          Surface entirely covered with small conical knobs (conules) that create the signature bumpy, warty, or granular texture.
•          Scattered, membranous, flush or slightly elevated oscula distributed across the surface.
•          Very soft and compressible tissue, easily torn or fragmented by water movement or contact.
•          Colonies typically spread 10 to 30 cm across.
Color:
•          Bright orange to yellowish orange externally: vivid, unmistakable coloration visible even in dim light.
•          Consistently orange throughout internally: no color differentiation between outer and inner tissue.
•          Uniform color saturation without patches, banding, or pale areas.
•          No bleaching or color variation even in deeper or shadier locations.
•          Color intensity provides immediate field identification as one of the most orange sponges on the reef.
Surface features:
•          Densely conulose: the entire surface is covered with tiny cone-like projections numbering in the hundreds per square centimeter.
•          Conules are roughly 1 to 3 mm in height, giving a granular, lumpy appearance rather than smooth, ridged, or spiky.
•          Scattered membranous oscula that are small and often flush or slightly recessed, difficult to distinguish without close inspection.
•          Texture reads as soft, compressible, and gelatinous: notably more fragile than other encrusting sponges.
•          Tissue easily torn or fragmented due to delicate construction and soft nature.
Visual context clues:
•          Commonly observed partially shaded or overgrown by adjacent corals or other encrusting organisms.
•          Bright orange stands out clearly against darker reef substrate and pale coral skeletons, visible from several meters away.
•          Often solitary or widely scattered rather than forming dense colonies, making individual specimens appear isolated.
•          Frequently hosts small fish or invertebrate associates that shelter within the conular surface.
•          The vivid color contrasting with adjacent dark reef organisms creates a recognizable visual signature.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Bright orange combined with bumpy conulose texture is diagnostic at first glance, recognizable instantly in any photograph.
•          Uniformly orange coloration without red tones, yellow tones, or banding distinguishes it from Monanchora arbuscula (red/scarlet variants).
•          Distinguished from Monanchora arbuscula (darker red, white-collared oscula, usually deeper) by color shade, oscula arrangement, and overall brightness.
•          Uniformly orange coloration plus lumpy form rules out most other small encrusting sponges in the Caribbean.
•          The combination of bright orange plus dense conules is essentially diagnostic and rarely confused with other species.
-----

species.name: Siphonodictyon xamaycaense
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A cryptic, encrusting boring sponge that inhabits cavities within coral skeletons and limestone rock, with visible oscular tubes and inhalant fistules projecting from the surface in scattered clusters. The epilithic portions appear as pale tan to whitish protrusions, while the endolithic tissue remains concealed within the substrate. In profile, the visible tubes are short, closed at the apex (in the case of fistules), and irregularly spaced across a colonized surface. The sponge’s true extent is difficult to assess visually because the majority of the tissue lies excavated within the rock matrix, making field identification dependent on recognizing the small, discrete chimney projections.
Growth form:
•          Tissue fills endolithic cavities and tunnel networks within the host rock or coral, connected to the surface by discrete tubes and fistules.
•          Oscular tubes are cylindrical, erect or slightly curved, and less than 5 mm in diameter, projecting from the substrate.
•          Inhalant fistules are apically closed, tubular structures that remain mostly concealed within surface pores.
•          Growth pattern is cryptic and irregular, following the available space within cavities rather than forming a cohesive external shape.
•          Fistules often appear in clusters or scattered groups rather than a uniform distribution.
•          Visible chimneys are solitary and separated, not joining or branching.
Color:
•          Outer tissue and epilithic tubes are tan, pale yellow, or cream colored when freshly exposed.
•          Interior excavated tissue is whitish to pale buff, difficult to observe without breaking the sponge.
•          The sponge may appear slightly darker or greenish-tinted when covered with algae or biofilm in situ.
•          Almost translucent at the tube edges where tissue is thinnest.
•          Often difficult to distinguish from surrounding pale coral at first glance.
Surface features:
•          The colonized rock surface shows scattered pores and small tube openings, creating a bumpy, stippled appearance.
•          Oscular mounds are low and irregular, without prominent projections.
•          The skeleton is not visible externally except as texture variation on the rock surface.
•          Fine surface texture of visible tubes is smooth to slightly granular.
•          Chimney may have a slight rim or collar at the opening, appearing as a subtle lip.
•          Very minimal external surface: most of the sponge body is hidden within the excavated chamber.
Visual context clues:
•          Always found occupying cavities in broken coral or limestone, never free-living or forming large external structures.
•          The pale tubes are visible only when the containing rock is turned or broken, revealing the hidden tissue network.
•          Rock surface colonized by the sponge often shows multiple species of boring organisms including other Siphonodictyon species.
•          Often hidden within or under coral plates and overhangs, with the chimney position the only visible clue to its presence.
•          Part of a coral bioeroding community alongside other cryptic sponges.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Small pale chimney protruding from coral or rubble surface is the defining field character.
•          Distinguished from Siphonodictyon coralliphagum by smaller tube diameter and paler coloration; S. coralliphagum has larger, more prominent fistules.
•          Single, unbranched tube opening that never bifurcates or produces secondary projections.
•          Cream to white coloration that is visually distinct from surrounding darker coral once located.
•          Found exclusively embedded in or on coral substrate, never on sand or isolated from reef structure.
-----

species.name: Smenospongia aurea
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A massive, lobate to tubular sponge with a distinctive layered mound structure, forming prominent rounded hillocks or dome-shaped colonies often with elevated oscular craters or volcano-like projections. The surface is rough and bumpy, covered with regularly spaced oscular openings that appear as dark spots or depressions against the lighter background. The sponge displays a striking color contrast between its drab tan to brown skin and its bright yellow, orange, or greenish-yellow oscules and interior flesh, creating a visually distinctive two-tone appearance.
Growth form:
•          Massive base with prominent oscular mounds or volcanic cones, each 1 to 3 cm in diameter, extending from a common foundation.
•          Mounds are rounded and bulbous, sometimes clustered in groups of 3 to 8 adjacent peaks, occasionally merging at the base.
•          Growth occurs primarily upward and outward, with older areas at the base and new mounds developing on top.
•          Individual oscular tubes are short, stout, and non-branching, embedded within the massive tissue.
•          Colonies may form isolated hemispherical masses or sprawling aggregations covering several square meters.
Color:
•          Variable overall: brown or drab tan skin with bright yellow, orange, or greenish-yellow oscules and interior flesh.
•          Yellow coloration is particularly prominent around oscular openings and on exposed interior surfaces.
•          Some populations show entirely greenish or olive skin, while others are deep brown with bright green interior.
•          The sponge becomes darker and exudes abundant mucus when handled, temporarily obscuring true color.
•          The two-tone appearance of dark exterior and bright yellow interior is the most distinctive color feature.
Surface features:
•          Surface covered with densely packed oscular pits, each 1 to 2 mm in diameter, arranged in an irregular but relatively even pattern.
•          Texture is rough and bumpy, with the skin having a coarse, honeycomb appearance when examined closely.
•          Dermis exhibits a characteristic honeycomb pattern when sectioned, visible as small areoles.
•          Small secondary ridges or radial patterns may radiate outward from each oscular mound.
•          The surface lacks gloss, appearing matte and granular.
Visual context clues:
•          Often found in high-energy surge zones and on exposed reef slopes, where it stands out as prominent yellow-capped mounds.
•          Frequently mixed with other massive sponges and coral rubble.
•          The bright yellow oscules are highly visible even in moderate lighting conditions, serving as a key field marker.
•          Often partially covered with algae or turf in shallow water, which can obscure the underlying mounds.
•          Colonies are too firm and brittle to compress, characteristic of dense compact sponges.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Distinguished from related sponges by the presence of distinct oscular mounds with bright yellow centres rather than diffuse conular tubers covering the entire surface.
•          Differs from other massive sponges by the bright yellow interior coloration visible around oscular openings, which is consistently more saturated than in related species.
•          The regular spacing and size of oscular features sets it apart from haphazardly arranged pores in encrusting competitors.
•          The firm, resistant texture and prominent mound growth form distinguish it from softer, more flaccid sponges.
-----

species.name: Spirastrella coccinea
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A thin, leathery encrusting sponge forming smooth, sheet-like patches that can cover entire rock surfaces over a square meter or more. The surface is uniformly flat to very slightly convex, appearing almost skin-like when spread across substrate. Oscular openings are clearly visible as small raised mounds or crater-like depressions, often arranged in an irregular but discernible pattern. The overall color is vibrant red to orange-red, with darker brownish or orange interiors visible at colony edges or damaged areas. The sponge has a waxy or slightly shiny appearance in bright light.
Growth form:
•          Encrusting form, less than 10 mm thick, spreading laterally across substrate as a continuous sheet.
•          Oscular mounds are slightly raised, roughly conical or dome-shaped, each approximately 1 to 2 mm in diameter.
•          Oscula are often arranged in a loose circular or spiral pattern, with transparent star-shaped canals radiating from each opening.
•          Growth margin is thin and advancing, with the sponge gradually consuming substrate and spreading outward from initial settlement points.
•          Colonies are non-branching, completely planar to the substrate, with no upright or tubular projections.
Color:
•          Bright vermillion to deep orange-red on the outer surface, with consistent coloration across the entire colony.
•          Interior and edges reveal brownish-red or darker orange flesh, indicating pigmentation concentrated in the ectosome.
•          Shallow-water specimens are typically orangish-red or coral-red, while deeper specimens shift toward pure red or deep crimson.
•          Surface may display white or pale specks near oscula, particularly in deeper colonies.
•          No secondary color patterns or stripes: coloration is homogeneous across the encrusting surface.
Surface features:
•          Texture is smooth and leathery, with a tight, uniform surface lacking visible pores except at oscular sites.
•          Oscula are the only prominent surface features, appearing as small raised bumps or depressions with crisp margins.
•          Radiating star-shaped canals extend from each osculum on the surface, visible as fine transparent grooves or ridges.
•          The sponge is not friable: the surface is tough and resistant to abrasion.
•          Surface has a slight gloss in good lighting, distinguishing it from matte encrusting species.
Visual context clues:
•          Frequently interspersed with zoanthids, soft corals, and other encrusting fauna, creating a patchwork of competing species.
•          The bright red color is unmistakable even in photographs taken at moderate distances.
•          Often covers considerable vertical surface area, appearing as vivid red stains or spreads across rock and coral.
•          Smooth uniform surface stands out among bumpy or pitted encrusting sponges.
•          The colony conforms tightly to substrate contours, never lifting or buckling.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Distinguished from Spirastrella hartmani by smaller size, thinner profile, and brighter red coloration; hartmani is thicker, more tan-orange, and has a more prominent vein star pattern.
•          Differs from thin encrusting tunicates (sea squirts) by the true sponge texture, lack of muscle-driven closure mechanisms, and consistent oscular patterns.
•          Separated from red/orange tubastraea corals by the sponge’s smooth, leathery surface versus the coral’s distinct polyp structure.
•          The radiating star pattern around oscula is a diagnostic feature not present in similar-appearing encrusting sponges.
-----

species.name: Spirastrella hartmani
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A thick, prominent encrusting sponge forming extensive patch-work expansions with conspicuous elevated vein-like ridges running across the surface, creating a distinctive net or chain-link pattern. The surface is bumpy and ridged rather than smooth, with raised exhalant canals forming the primary visual texture. The growth is generally planar to substrate but with more topographic relief than related encrusting species. The base color is salmon to dull orange, with prominent dark brown or burgundy vein markings that provide strong visual contrast. Colonies can reach approximately 1 meter in diameter and spread across large areas of reef.
Growth form:
•          Thick encrusting sheet, typically 5 to 15 mm in depth, much thicker than S. coccinea.
•          Oscular openings are embedded in conspicuous elevated ridges, forming a star or vein-like pattern across the surface.
•          Exhalant canals are prominent linear features, running across the sponge surface in a branching or reticulate arrangement.
•          Growth pattern is spreading and accretionary, advancing outward from central settlement points while maintaining consistent thickness.
•          Surface relief can be pronounced, with ridges protruding 2 to 3 mm above the surrounding tissue.
Color:
•          Base color is salmon, tan-orange, or muted orange, less vibrant than S. coccinea.
•          Exhalant vein ridges are dark brown, burgundy, or blackish, providing sharp contrast against the lighter background.
•          Interior flesh is orange to burnt orange, visible at colony edges or damage sites.
•          Coloration is relatively stable across depth and geographic range, less variable than in Smenospongia species.
•          The vein-to-base color contrast is the most distinctive visual feature.
Surface features:
•          Elevated vein ridges form the dominant surface texture, arranged in a somewhat regular but intricate branching pattern across the sponge.
•          Oscula are embedded within or at the intersections of the vein network.
•          Surface texture is rough to moderately bumpy, with pronounced topography relative to other encrusting sponges.
•          The vein pattern creates small chambers or compartments on the surface, giving a net-like appearance.
•          Fine surface detail shows smooth tissue between ridges but coarse, prominent skeletal features at the ridge crests.
Visual context clues:
•          Frequently associated with rock formations and coral rubble rather than living coral surfaces.
•          The vein pattern is distinctive at distance, visible in wide-angle reef photographs.
•          Often partially shaded or in areas of moderate water flow, less common on open surge-exposed surfaces.
•          Colonies may be heavily fouled with algae, which can obscure the color contrast but does not hide the vein pattern.
•          The honeycomb-like ridge network is the primary visual signature, recognizable even from several meters.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Distinguished from Spirastrella coccinea by the much thicker encrustation, elevated vein ridges, and darker coloration; coccinea is thin, smooth, and bright red.
•          Differs from Smenospongia aurea by the thinner profile, lack of prominent oscular mounds, and presence of distinctive vein markings that aurea does not display.
•          Separated from other encrusting sponges by the characteristic dark brown vein network forming a unique reticulate surface pattern.
•          The vein-star pattern around oscula is more linear and pronounced than in S. coccinea.
-----

species.name: Svenzea zeai
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A massive, branching to lobate sponge with thick, robust tubes or columnar projections ranging from slightly flattened cylinders to bulbous lobes. The growth form is predominantly upright and sculptural, with one to several prominent vertical or semi-vertical branches arising from a common base or spreading encrusting foundation. The surface is heavily pitted or punctate, covered with numerous small oscular openings creating a pock-marked, textured appearance. The overall color is deep purple to burgundy, sometimes with darker brown or blackish tones, and the sponge often appears heavy and dense.
Growth form:
•          Massive base, often flattened or encrusting, giving rise to prominent upright branches or tubes.
•          Branches are thick and robust, typically 5 to 15 cm in diameter, sometimes flattened or slightly compressed.
•          Branch arrangement is relatively sparse, with branches widely spaced rather than clustered.
•          Growth occurs primarily vertically, creating a distinctive sculptural silhouette when viewed in profile.
•          Surface is heavily pitted with oscular pores, distributed across the entire branch and base surface.
•          Colonies range widely in size, from small starter colonies to specimens exceeding 30 cm in height.
Color:
•          Deep purple to dark burgundy, the most consistent and recognizable field marker for the species.
•          Some specimens shift toward brown-purple or blackish-purple in deeper water or high-energy sites.
•          Interior flesh is deep purple or maroon, visible at damaged sites.
•          Color is relatively uniform across the sponge; no distinctive color banding or sectioning.
•          The sponge turns nearly black in air and becomes dusky or nearly invisible in deep water.
Surface features:
•          Densely pitted surface with oscular pores, each 0.5 to 1.5 mm in diameter, arranged in an irregular but comprehensive pattern.
•          Pits appear as dark dots or small craters, creating a rough, pocked texture across the entire surface.
•          Surface detail shows short spongin fiber networks in some specimens, forming a visible honeycomb or lattice texture.
•          The skeleton is composed mainly of short, stout styles arranged in isodictyal reticulation, but this is not visually apparent without sectioning.
•          Fine surface texture is leathery and somewhat fragile, with tissue easily damaged or eroding in situ.
Visual context clues:
•          Frequently nestled in coral rubble or attached to coral lower skeleton, often in shaded or cryptic microsites.
•          The deep purple color is distinctive even in poor lighting, a key field identification feature.
•          Often encountered singly rather than in dense aggregations, though multiple colonies may occupy the same coral head.
•          Sponge exudes noticeable mucus when touched and is soft and easily fragmented compared to other branching sponges.
•          The dark silhouette against pale coral skeleton creates a recognizable visual contrast.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Distinguished from Svenzea flava (yellow volcano sponge) by deep purple coloration versus flava’s bright pale yellow or golden hue.
•          Differs from Svenzea tubulosa by the shorter, more compact branches and more uniform pitted surface versus tubulosa’s longer, more linear tubes with larger oscular openings.
•          Separated from Svenzea cristinae by the darker purple color and more robust growth form; cristinae is paler and more delicate.
•          The deep purple color is incompatible with any other common Caribbean sponge, making it instantly recognizable in field conditions.
-----

species.name: Verongula rigida
species.description:
Visual description
Overall appearance:
A massive to lobate sponge with a highly variable growth form, appearing either as low, irregularly arranged dome-shaped mounds, thick repent branches or runners, or occasionally as distinct upright tubes or cones projecting from a common flattened base. The surface is heavily textured with visible honeycomb or lattice patterns created by exposed spongin fiber networks. The surface is never smooth, with prominent irregular ridging and pitting throughout. The base color is bright light to dark green, while the interior flesh is lemon yellow or pale yellow-orange, creating a striking color contrast visible at broken edges. The sponge is quite firm and rigid (hence the specific epithet), with a somewhat brittle or flaking texture.
Growth form:
•          Massive base, often flattened or crustose, from which irregular lobes or thick branches extend.
•          Where exposed, branches are thick and robust, appearing as 5 to 10 cm tall columnar or conical projections.
•          Oscular openings are arranged in somewhat regular groups or aligned rows along the tops of mounds or branch crests.
•          Growth is irregular and asymmetrical, following available space rather than forming a predictable shape.
•          In wave-exposed sites, the sponge becomes flattened and repent, appearing as thick, undulating runners rather than upright branches.
Color:
•          Bright light to dark green on outer surfaces, with considerable variation in shade depending on depth and lighting.
•          Lemon yellow to pale orange-yellow on interior flesh and exposed surfaces.
•          The green-to-yellow color contrast at damaged edges is a distinctive diagnostic feature.
•          Surface green may have slight brownish or olive tones, particularly in deep water.
•          The sponge turns purple or reddish when exposed to air, a notable field observation used to verify identification.
Surface features:
•          Prominent honeycomb or lattice texture formed by exposed spongin fiber networks creating the walls of chambers.
•          Small oscular openings are regularly distributed along branch crests, appearing as dark spots or small depressions.
•          Surface is never smooth or leathery, always showing coarse, fibrous skeletal texture.
•          Spongin fibers are visibly golden or tan-colored, contrasting with the green tissue.
•          Fine detail shows irregular pitting and ridging, with the fiber network creating a “basket-weave” or honeycomb appearance.
Visual context clues:
•          Often scattered among other sponges and coral rubble, appearing as prominent green mounds in a diverse benthic landscape.
•          The bright green color is highly visible even in wide-angle underwater photography, standing out sharply against darker sponges.
•          Frequently encrusted with algae or tunicates, which may partially obscure the color but does not hide the characteristic fiber network texture.
•          The sponge’s firmness and brittleness are notable when encountered; it does not compress or deform like softer sponges.
•          The green mound silhouette against pale coral or sand is a recognizable visual cue.
Diagnostic look in photos:
•          Distinguished from Verongula gigantea (giant tube sponge) by much smaller size, green rather than purple coloration, and lack of large oscular tubes; gigantea is massive and tubular with purple or reddish interiors.
•          Differs from Verongula reiswigi by bright green coloration versus reiswigi’s darker green or brown, and more irregular mound structure versus reiswigi’s more organized tube arrangements.
•          Separated from other green encrusting sponges by the highly prominent honeycomb fiber texture and lemon-yellow interior, features not evident in smooth, dense encrusting competitors.
•          The visible spongin fiber network is a diagnostic feature that distinguishes Verongula from nearly all other sponges.
